analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate how AFB1, a common feed mycotoxin, affects viral infections, particularly its potential to worsen the impact of H3N8 avian influenza on poultry gut health.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted in vitro and in vivo using environmentally relevant AFB1 levels (25–100 μg/kg) and focused on H3N8 avian influenza in chickens.
analysis.methods: The researchers used integrated histopathological, microbiome, and metabolomic analyses to assess the effects of AFB1 on gut barrier function and bacterial colonization in H3N8-infected chickens.
analysis.main_results: The analyses showed that AFB1 induced gut barrier dysfunction and specific depletion of beneficial bacteria such as Eubacterium and Subdoligranulum, with a reduction in dodecanedioic acid levels.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings reveal a novel mechanism by which AFB1 enhances H3N8 replication through disruption of intestinal homeostasis and SFB colonization, highlighting a previously unexplored interaction between mycotoxins and avian influenza.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results suggest that controlling AFB1 levels in poultry feed could be a critical strategy to reduce the risk of avian influenza outbreaks and improve gut health in birds.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to in vitro and in vivo models, and the evidence is based on abstract-level reporting, which may not fully capture in-field complexities. The evidence strength is moderate.

Mechanistically, AFB1 disrupts intestinal homeostasis by compromising mucosal integrity and SFB colonization, thereby amplifying H3N8 pathogenesis. The findings establish a novel mycotoxin-virus interaction axis through gut dysbiosis, emphasizing the need for AFB1 control strategies in poultry production to mitigate influenza risks. elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究使用环境相关的 AFB1 水平(25-100 μg/kg)在体外和体内进行,重点关注鸡中的 H3N8 禽流感。

elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果揭示了 AFB1 通过破坏肠道稳态和 SFB 定植来增强 H3N8 复制的新机制,强调了霉菌毒素和 禽流感 之间以前未探索过的相互作用。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果表明,控制家禽饲料中的 AFB1 水平可能是降低 禽流感 暴发 风险和改善家禽肠道健康的关键策略。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于体外和体内模型,证据基于抽象水平的报告,可能无法完全捕捉现场的复杂性。证据强度中等。

analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果揭示了 AFB1 通过破坏肠道稳态和 SFB 定植来增强 H3N8 复制的新机制,强调了霉菌毒素和 禽流感 之间以前未探索过的相互作用。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果表明,控制家禽饲料中的 AFB1 水平可能是降低 禽流感 暴发 风险和改善家禽肠道健康的关键策略。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于体外和体内模型,证据基于抽象水平的报告,可能无法完全捕捉现场的复杂性。证据强度中等。

Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search Support Menu 4 new human H9N2 avian flu cases in China as Australia sees more H5N1 in wild birds News brief August 4, 2026 Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Avian Influenza (Bird Flu) Share Juperiterimages / iStock Hong Kong's Centre for Health Protection (CHP) is reporting four new cases of H9N2 avian flu on mainland China. The case-patients include a 3-year-old girl from Gansu province, a 12-year-old boy from Jiangsu province, a 72-year-old woman from Jiangxi province, and a 58-year-old woman from Yunnan province. All patients had symptom onset between July 5 and July 13. CHP provided no additional information on the patients’ prognosis or course of illness. There have been 20 known human infections of H9N2 over the past six months, including 12 on mainland China, one each in Hong Kong and Taiwan, and one case in Italy. Since 2015, a total of 164 cases of human infection with H9N2 avian flu, including two deaths (both in people with underlying conditions), have been reported to the World Health Organization in the Western Pacific, the organization said. Australia now has 102 wild bird detections of H5N1 In other avian flu news, Australia is reporting scores of new wild bird detections of H5N1 in the weeks following the virus’ introduction to the continent. Between July 20 and today, detections rose from 20 to 102, with the majority of detections in South Australia. So far Australia has not detected the virus in poultry or the wider agriculture industry. Review: Self-collected HPV tests accurately detect pre-cancerous cells in women News brief August 4, 2026 Meghan Holohan Topics Human Papillomavirus (HPV) anastas / iStock A meta-analysis of 11 studies concludes that self-testing for human papilloma virus (HPV) using urine or vaginal samples accurately detects pre-cancerous cells caused by HPV, also known as high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL+). This paper, published in the Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Research, reinforces the precision of self-collection testing for HPV, which could increase access to screening. “The outcomes of this investigation indicate that HPV testing performed using both self-collected urine specimen and vaginal specimens achieved a high sensitivity in detecting HSIL+,” wrote the Taiwanese authors. High sensitivity for self-collected vaginal swabs The World Health Organization (WHO) hopes to eliminate cervical cancer by 2030 and sees HPV self-collecting kits as one way to expand screening to reach more women, especially those who have not yet undergone HPV testing. The researchers hoped to understand the accuracy of self-testing methods by looking at studies that examined the precision of self-collected HPV kits in finding abnormal cells using urine or vaginal samples. The papers included in the analysis were based on 3,534 self-collected urine samples and 3,523 vaginal samples. The distribution of self-sampling kits has the potential to yield a low rate of adverse events and a high level of satisfaction among patients. Self-collection of urine samples had a pooled sensitivity of 81%, while self-testing with vaginal swabs had a pooled sensitivity of 88.6% for detecting pre-cancerous cells. “The meta-analysis corroborated the high sensitivity of HPV testing with self-collected vaginal specimens,” the authors wrote. “The distribution of self-sampling kits has the potential to yield a low rate of adverse events and a high level of satisfaction among patients.” Climate change is shifting malaria activity in Africa News brief August 4, 2026 Sarah Boden Topics Malaria Climate change is moving where the malaria hotbeds are in Africa, forcing new regions to contend with the mosquito-borne disease. The female Anopheles stephensi mosquito transmits malaria parasites. Credit: James Gathany / CDC Both the malaria parasite and the life cycle of the mosquito vectors, which are cold-blooded, are highly responsive to temperatures, making the disease sensitive to climate change. A recent study in Nature finds that rising temperatures have likely increased malaria in high-elevation East and southern Africa, where the weather is typically cooler. At the same time, climate change likely averted a comparable number of cases in West Africa, where temperatures are increasing to a point that it's hot enough to reduce transmission. The analysis used 50,425 surveys of malaria infection rates in sub-Saharan Africa, spanning 1900–2016, to calculate monthly averages of the disease at the state or province level. Then, researchers modeled how temperature and extreme precipitation shaped the prevalence of malaria in each region, controlling for factors like seasonality and malaria intervention efforts. "Over the coming century, we project that climate change could marginally accelerate the elimination of malaria in West and central Africa, where the present-day burden is highest," write the study authors, which include researchers from Yale University, the University of California, Berkeley, and the University of Cape Town. Malaria mitigation efforts have a larger impact than climate change Although the effects of climate change on malaria are meaningful, the authors caution that the impact is far smaller than the reductions that have been achieved through medical care, mosquito nets, vector control, and economic development. These investments, they argue, can counterbalance the effects of climate change in most places. "Malaria elimination within the next generation remains plausible, even in the face of climate change," they said. They add that future work should explore how emerging methods for predicting climate change could give public health agencies valuable information in preparing for and responding to malaria activity. More than one-third of invasive E coli isolates are multidrug-resistant, global analysis finds News brief August 4, 2026 Chris Dall, MA Topics Antimicrobial Stewardship E coli An analysis of invasive Escherichia coli isolates collected from 26 countries found that more than one-third were multidrug-resistant (MDR), researchers reported today in Clinical Infectious Diseases. CDC / Alissa Eckert The study, by researchers with drugmaker Johnson & Johnson, analyzed more than 10,000 E coli isolates collected from patients with bloodstream infections from 2011 through 2023. The aim of the study was to evaluate the antibiotic resistance, sequence type (ST), and O-serotype distribution of extraintestinal pathogenic E coli (ExPEC), a pathogen that can infect sites outside the intestines and cause invasive E coli disease, or IED, which includes life-threatening conditions like sepsis. “Increasing antimicrobial resistance rates and the emergence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) E. coli strains represent a major challenge in the treatment of IED,” the study authors wrote. “In particular, resistance to carbapenems, third-generation cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, or fluoroquinolones is an obstacle to successful treatment.” 34% of E coli isolates labeled as MDR Of the 10,098 ExPEC isolates collected, 34% were labeled as MDR, but there was a wide variation between countries. India had the highest MDR rate (83.3%), followed by Mexico (76.6%) and China (69.4%), while the Netherlands (12.1%), New Zealand (11.6%), and Sweden (10.6%) had the lowest MDR rates. Countries with lower income levels tended to have higher rates of MDR E coli. Overall, serotypes O25, O2, O6, and O1 were the most prevalent. Among the MDR isolates, O25 was the most prevalent in all countries (ranging from 11.3% in China to 56.2% in Mexico). ST131, a globally dominant clone and important cause of urinary tract and bloodstream infections worldwide, accounted for 33% of all MDR isolates. “Our findings stress the importance of epidemiological studies to monitor the prevalence of high-risk ExPEC clones and highlight the need for ongoing research into novel preventive and therapeutic strategies, including vaccines, to reduce the burden of bacterial disease and limit the spread of antimicrobial resistance,” the authors concluded. The case-patients include a 3-year-old girl from Gansu province, a 12-year-old boy from Jiangsu province, a 72-year-old woman from Jiangxi province, and a 58-year-old woman from Yunnan province. All patients had symptom onset between July 5 and July 13. CHP provided no additional information on the patients’ prognosis or course of illness. There have been 20 known human infections of H9N2 over the past six months, including 12 on mainland China, one each in Hong Kong and Taiwan, and one case in Italy. Since 2015, a total of 164 cases of human infection with H9N2 avian flu, including two deaths (both in people with underlying conditions), have been reported to the World Health Organization in the Western Pacific, the organization said. Australia now has 102 wild bird detections of H5N1 In other avian flu news, Australia is reporting scores of new wild bird detections of H5N1 in the weeks following the virus’ introduction to the continent. Between July 20 and today, detections rose from 20 to 102, with the majority of detections in South Australia. So far Australia has not detected the virus in poultry or the wider agriculture industry. Review: Self-collected HPV tests accurately detect pre-cancerous cells in women News brief August 4, 2026 Meghan Holohan Topics Human Papillomavirus (HPV) anastas / iStock A meta-analysis of 11 studies concludes that self-testing for human papilloma virus (HPV) using urine or vaginal samples accurately detects pre-cancerous cells caused by HPV, also known as high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL+). This paper, published in the Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Research, reinforces the precision of self-collection testing for HPV, which could increase access to screening. “The outcomes of this investigation indicate that HPV testing performed using both self-collected urine specimen and vaginal specimens achieved a high sensitivity in detecting HSIL+,” wrote the Taiwanese authors. High sensitivity for self-collected vaginal swabs The World Health Organization (WHO) hopes to eliminate cervical cancer by 2030 and sees HPV self-collecting kits as one way to expand screening to reach more women, especially those who have not yet undergone HPV testing. The researchers hoped to understand the accuracy of self-testing methods by looking at studies that examined the precision of self-collected HPV kits in finding abnormal cells using urine or vaginal samples. The papers included in the analysis were based on 3,534 self-collected urine samples and 3,523 vaginal samples. The distribution of self-sampling kits has the potential to yield a low rate of adverse events and a high level of satisfaction among patients. Self-collection of urine samples had a pooled sensitivity of 81%, while self-testing with vaginal swabs had a pooled sensitivity of 88.6% for detecting pre-cancerous cells. “The meta-analysis corroborated the high sensitivity of HPV testing with self-collected vaginal specimens,” the authors wrote. “The distribution of self-sampling kits has the potential to yield a low rate of adverse events and a high level of satisfaction among patients.” Climate change is shifting malaria activity in Africa News brief August 4, 2026 Sarah Boden Topics Malaria Climate change is moving where the malaria hotbeds are in Africa, forcing new regions to contend with the mosquito-borne disease. The female Anopheles stephensi mosquito transmits malaria parasites. Credit: James Gathany / CDC Both the malaria parasite and the life cycle of the mosquito vectors, which are cold-blooded, are highly responsive to temperatures, making the disease sensitive to climate change. A recent study in Nature finds that rising temperatures have likely increased malaria in high-elevation East and southern Africa, where the weather is typically cooler. At the same time, climate change likely averted a comparable number of cases in West Africa, where temperatures are increasing to a point that it's hot enough to reduce transmission. The analysis used 50,425 surveys of malaria infection rates in sub-Saharan Africa, spanning 1900–2016, to calculate monthly averages of the disease at the state or province level. Then, researchers modeled how temperature and extreme precipitation shaped the prevalence of malaria in each region, controlling for factors like seasonality and malaria intervention efforts. "Over the coming century, we project that climate change could marginally accelerate the elimination of malaria in West and central Africa, where the present-day burden is highest," write the study authors, which include researchers from Yale University, the University of California, Berkeley, and the University of Cape Town. Malaria mitigation efforts have a larger impact than climate change Although the effects of climate change on malaria are meaningful, the authors caution that the impact is far smaller than the reductions that have been achieved through medical care, mosquito nets, vector control, and economic development. These investments, they argue, can counterbalance the effects of climate change in most places. "Malaria elimination within the next generation remains plausible, even in the face of climate change," they said. They add that future work should explore how emerging methods for predicting climate change could give public health agencies valuable information in preparing for and responding to malaria activity. More than one-third of invasive E coli isolates are multidrug-resistant, global analysis finds News brief August 4, 2026 Chris Dall, MA Topics Antimicrobial Stewardship E coli An analysis of invasive Escherichia coli isolates collected from 26 countries found that more than one-third were multidrug-resistant (MDR), researchers reported today in Clinical Infectious Diseases. CDC / Alissa Eckert The study, by researchers with drugmaker Johnson & Johnson, analyzed more than 10,000 E coli isolates collected from patients with bloodstream infections from 2011 through 2023. The aim of the study was to evaluate the antibiotic resistance, sequence type (ST), and O-serotype distribution of extraintestinal pathogenic E coli (ExPEC), a pathogen that can infect sites outside the intestines and cause invasive E coli disease, or IED, which includes life-threatening conditions like sepsis. “Increasing antimicrobial resistance rates and the emergence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) E. coli strains represent a major challenge in the treatment of IED,” the study authors wrote. “In particular, resistance to carbapenems, third-generation cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, or fluoroquinolones is an obstacle to successful treatment.” 34% of E coli isolates labeled as MDR Of the 10,098 ExPEC isolates collected, 34% were labeled as MDR, but there was a wide variation between countries. India had the highest MDR rate (83.3%), followed by Mexico (76.6%) and China (69.4%), while the Netherlands (12.1%), New Zealand (11.6%), and Sweden (10.6%) had the lowest MDR rates. Countries with lower income levels tended to have higher rates of MDR E coli. Overall, serotypes O25, O2, O6, and O1 were the most prevalent. Among the MDR isolates, O25 was the most prevalent in all countries (ranging from 11.3% in China to 56.2% in Mexico). ST131, a globally dominant clone and important cause of urinary tract and bloodstream infections worldwide, accounted for 33% of all MDR isolates. “Our findings stress the importance of epidemiological studies to monitor the prevalence of high-risk ExPEC clones and highlight the need for ongoing research into novel preventive and therapeutic strategies, including vaccines, to reduce the burden of bacterial disease and limit the spread of antimicrobial resistance,” the authors concluded. news.content: AZ EN Region World AnewZ Originals AI & Next Business Culture Green Programmes Investigations Opinion Live Live Region World AnewZ Originals AI & Next Business Culture Green Programmes Investigations Opinion AnewZ Talks Follow Us Home Health Health news Bird Flu H5N1 bird flu kills dozens of seabirds as Australia warns of wider wildlife spread A test tube labelled "Bird Flu", eggs and a piece of paper in the colours of the Australian national flag are seen in this picture illustration, 14 January, 2023. reuters By Elnur Mirzazada , Reuters August 3, 2026 11:51 Copied Australia warned on Monday (3 August) of a wider spread of H5N1 bird flu after its first confirmed mass mortality event among seabirds killed about 50 greater crested terns off the coast of South Australia, south of Adelaide. Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said testing confirmed H5N1 in a group of 49 dead and 35 sick terns found during helicopter surveillance on rocks off Cape Jaffa, about 250 kilometres from Adelaide, on Friday. “Australians should expect to see more spread and larger numbers now of wildlife being affected,” Collins told reporters in Canberra. She said it was the first confirmed mass mortality event in Australia, warning that once H5 bird flu spreads through wildlife and the natural environment, significant losses cannot be avoided. Australia has recorded 74 confirmed cases across the country, from Western Australia to Queensland, although most have been in South Australia, Collins said. Farms remain unaffected There is no evidence so far of the virus on Australian farms, many of which have tightened biosecurity measures to protect poultry flocks since H5N1 was first detected in June. Australia and New Zealand, which confirmed its first H5N1 case last month, have spent years preparing for the virus through enhanced farm biosecurity, shorebird testing, vaccination of vulnerable species and response planning exercises. Human risk remains low The virus has killed hundreds of millions of birds and mammals in recent years, caused billions of U.S. dollars in losses for poultry farmers, infected cattle in the U.S. and left beaches littered with the bodies of birds and seals. H5N1 bird flu can infect humans who come into contact with infected animals, but global case numbers remain low and health officials say the risk to the public remains low. news.content_original: AZ EN Region World AnewZ Originals AI & Next Business Culture Green Programmes Investigations Opinion Live Live Region World AnewZ Originals AI & Next Business Culture Green Programmes Investigations Opinion AnewZ Talks Follow Us Home Health Health news Bird Flu H5N1 bird flu kills dozens of seabirds as Australia warns of wider wildlife spread A test tube labelled "Bird Flu", eggs and a piece of paper in the colours of the Australian national flag are seen in this picture illustration, 14 January, 2023. reuters By Elnur Mirzazada , Reuters August 3, 2026 11:51 Copied Australia warned on Monday (3 August) of a wider spread of H5N1 bird flu after its first confirmed mass mortality event among seabirds killed about 50 greater crested terns off the coast of South Australia, south of Adelaide. Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said testing confirmed H5N1 in a group of 49 dead and 35 sick terns found during helicopter surveillance on rocks off Cape Jaffa, about 250 kilometres from Adelaide, on Friday. “Australians should expect to see more spread and larger numbers now of wildlife being affected,” Collins told reporters in Canberra. She said it was the first confirmed mass mortality event in Australia, warning that once H5 bird flu spreads through wildlife and the natural environment, significant losses cannot be avoided. Australia has recorded 74 confirmed cases across the country, from Western Australia to Queensland, although most have been in South Australia, Collins said. Farms remain unaffected There is no evidence so far of the virus on Australian farms, many of which have tightened biosecurity measures to protect poultry flocks since H5N1 was first detected in June. Australia and New Zealand, which confirmed its first H5N1 case last month, have spent years preparing for the virus through enhanced farm biosecurity, shorebird testing, vaccination of vulnerable species and response planning exercises. Human risk remains low The virus has killed hundreds of millions of birds and mammals in recent years, caused billions of U.S. dollars in losses for poultry farmers, infected cattle in the U.S. and left beaches littered with the bodies of birds and seals. H5N1 bird flu can infect humans who come into contact with infected animals, but global case numbers remain low and health officials say the risk to the public remains low. news.content_title: Bird Flu Kills 84 Terns at Baudin Rock as Silver Gulls Threaten to Carry H5N1 Inland
news.content: Aerial surveillance crews scanning a remote South Australian islet on Friday, August 1, counted 49 dead greater crested terns and 35 more showing acute signs of illness — the largest single-site bird flu casualty count Australia has ever recorded, according to the federal H5 bird flu dashboard . In the same news cycle, a silver gull found at Robe became the first of its species anywhere in Australia to test positive for H5N1 , a development wildlife experts immediately identified as something qualitatively different from anything that had come before. South Australia's Chief Veterinary Officer Skye Fruean said it was "very unlikely" the terns at Baudin Rock — a protected islet about 5 kilometres (3.1 miles) south of Cape Jaffa — would test negative for H5. Laboratory confirmation from CSIRO's Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness was still pending at the time of reporting, but Fruean described the scene in terms that left little ambiguity: "We've known that this is going to happen at some point in time. Unfortunately, it does appear to be escalating quite rapidly ." Australia Just Crossed a Threshold It Cannot Walk Back From As of 9am Australian Eastern Standard Time on August 2, Australia had confirmed 54 H5 detections in wild seabirds across five states, according to the DAFF bird flu monitoring page . That count rose from 53 just hours earlier when six new cases were confirmed in Victoria — four in Portland and two in Nelson Bay — marking the first confirmed detections in that state. South Australia accounts for 39 of the national total, making it by far the outbreak's epicenter. The accelerating case count is not the most significant development. It is the pattern the cases reveal. The 19 greater crested terns confirmed positive over the 24 hours prior to the Baudin Rock discovery were collected from scattered points across the Limestone Coast and Kangaroo Island, including Beachport, Cape Jaffa, Southend, Port MacDonnell, Robe, and Seal Bay, as detailed in South Australia's H5 bird flu testing updates . That geographic dispersal, across multiple sites rather than a single point of entry, is the signature of established local, bird-to-bird transmission — not a new incursion from a migratory arrival. Australia's authorities confirmed this explicitly. The national decision that H5N1 is "no longer technically feasible to eradicate in wildlife" was made before this week's events. Why the Silver Gull Changes Everything The greater crested tern is a seabird. It nests on offshore islands, forages in coastal and open ocean waters, and moves primarily along the shoreline. When terns die in large numbers on a protected islet, the tragedy is real but geographically bounded. The virus stays near the water it arrived from. The silver gull ( Chroicocephalus novaehollandiae ) does not stay near the water. Australia's most familiar seabird is found on every beach, coastal suburb, rubbish tip, inland wetland, and freshwater reservoir in the country. It ranges from the shoreline into agricultural zones and urban centers. More critically for the current outbreak, it is a scavenger — a bird that eats what other birds leave behind, including carcasses . Sean Dooley, national affairs adviser at BirdLife Australia, identified the implication precisely. "There is such a large population of silver gulls, and they move into other habitats. They could be the vector that takes bird flu inland ," Dooley said. He noted that silver gulls "do come inland and can turn up in Lake Eyre following floods" — pointing to a geographic reach that dwarfs anything the tern population alone could achieve. Suman Majumdar, chief health officer at the Burnet Institute, was more direct about the mechanism: "Gulls move between beaches, wetlands, farmland and urban areas, which could carry the virus into a much wider range of wildlife, poultry and environments," Majumdar told AAP . What makes this especially concerning is not only the gull's range but the ecological pathway through which it acquires the virus. When infected terns die on beaches and islands, silver gulls scavenge the carcasses. Research from the South American outbreak documented exactly this process — where, as scientists described, "gull scavenging of pinniped carcasses and nesting on beaches amidst hundreds of tern carcasses" created sustained transmission cycles between species that would not otherwise have had direct contact. The silver gull detection in Australia signals that this same relay mechanism has now begun. Seal Bay: Where the Math Gets Frightening Of the 19 terns confirmed positive in the same 24-hour window as the Baudin Rock mass mortality event, five were found at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island . Seal Bay is not merely another stretch of South Australian coastline. It is one of the most critical breeding grounds for the Australian sea lion ( Neophoca cinerea ) , a species listed as endangered under both Australian federal law and the IUCN Red List, with an estimated total global population of approximately 14,730 individuals. Wayne Boardman, a wildlife veterinarian at the University of Adelaide, did not soften his assessment. "The issue now with bird flu being found at Seal Bay is that it's almost certainly going to go from the birds into the sea lions," Boardman told the ABC . analysis_en.time: Event date: August 1, 2026 (aerial surveillance); Publication date: August 2, 2026 (Tech Times). Time range: 24-hour period prior to August 1 and confirmed by 9am AEST August 2.
analysis_en.location_and_population: Baudin Rock (protected islet ~5 km south of Cape Jaffa, South Australia); Seal Bay, Kangaroo Island; Beachport, Cape Jaffa, Southend, Port MacDonnell, Robe, Nelson Bay, Portland (Victoria); Robe (South Australia). analysis_en.event: Australia's first confirmed H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b outbreak in wild seabirds, with rapid local transmission and spillover risk to mammals. analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: 84 dead greater crested terns at Baudin Rock (49 confirmed dead, 35 acutely ill); 54 H5 detections in wild seabirds across five Australian states as of 9am AEST August 2 (39 in South Australia, 6 new in Victoria); 19 greater crested terns confirmed positive in prior 24 hours across multiple South Australian sites.

news.title_zh: 银鸥威胁将 H5N1 病毒带入内陆,导致博丹岩 84 只燕鸥死亡 - 科技时报
news.source_body_en: Australia confirmed its first H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b outbreak in wild seabirds on August 1, 2026, after aerial crews counted 84 dead greater crested terns and 35 acutely ill at Baudin Rock, a protected islet off South Australia. The national tally reached 54 H5 detections across five states by August 2, with 39 in South Australia alone. Wildlife experts warn the outbreak is escalating rapidly, with local bird-to-bird transmission now established across multiple coastal sites. The silver gull, Australia’s ubiquitous scavenger, is identified as a key vector that could carry the virus inland and into urban areas. Of greatest concern, endangered Australian sea lions at Seal Bay face imminent spillover risk from infected tern carcasses, mirroring catastrophic mortality events in South America and on sub-Antarctic Heard Island, where H5N1 killed 76% of southern elephant seal pups. CSIRO is conducting confirmatory tests, while South Australia has suspended beach tours at Seal Bay to limit human disturbance.

Home Arts + Culture Economy Education Environment + Energy Ethics + Religion Health Politics + Society Science + Tech World Podcasts Local En Español Edition Africa Australia Brasil Canada Canada (français) Català España Europe France Global Indonesia New Zealand United Kingdom United States Donate Skip to content Edition: United States Africa Australia Brasil Canada Canada (français) Català España Europe France Global Indonesia New Zealand United Kingdom s Donate Newsletters Become an author Sign up as a reader Sign in Academic rigor, journalistic flair Arts + Culture Economy Education Environment + Energy Ethics + Religion Health Politics + Society Science + Tech World Podcasts Local Thomas Parker/pexels The warning signs are over: Australia now faces a devastating bird flu outbreak in wildlife Published: August 1, 2026 6:38pm EDT The spread of H5N1 birdflu is worsening. At the time of writing, Australia has 53 confirmed detections in wild seabirds across five states. In South Australia there are 39 confirmed cases, including a silver gull at Robe and 19 greater crested terns found along the Limestone Coast and Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island. South Australian authorities are also investigating 49 dead and 35 sick greater crested terns found by aerial surveillance teams at an offshore location south of Cape Jaffa. Samples are still being tested, but if confirmed, this would represent the first mass mortality of Australian animals associated with the virus. Until recently, Australia’s detections were mostly isolated migratory seabirds arriving from the Southern Ocean. But these detections show this has changed, with local transmission among wildlife that live in Australia. Which species are most at risk? Animals that gather densely in breeding colonies face the greatest danger. Terns, gulls, gannets and albatrosses can transmit the virus rapidly through close contact and contaminated environments, with these groups experiencing devastating mortality in other parts of the world. The silver gull infections are particularly concerning because they move between beaches, towns, rubbish tips, wetlands and inland waterways. A suspected case at Monarto, SA, does not prove H5N1 is yet established inland, but it shows infected seabirds cannot be “coastally contained”. Seals and sea lions also require urgent surveillance. H5N1 killed more than 17,000 southern elephant seals in Argentina in 2023, with 95% pup mortality at one monitored colony. Around 13,000 elephant seal pups later died on Heard Island. While it was not possible to carry out postmortem examinations on all individuals at this remote location, H5N1 was confirmed as present and recorded as the most likely cause of death. Five infected terns have now been confirmed at Seal Bay, a critical breeding site for the endangered Australian sea lion. Australian sea lions and fur seals breed in dense colonies where disease could spread quickly. Australian sea lions on a beach in South Australia. Seals and sea lions require urgent surveillance - many thousands have died from H5N1 overseas. Phil Kirkpatrick/flickr, CC BY Can we predict how far it will spread? We cannot reliably predict the spread of H5N1 in Australia. The 53 confirmed detections are not the true number of infections – they are the birds found, reported and tested. Many infected animals will never be detected. Cases from the rest of the world show this strain of H5N1 is capable of spreading huge distances, carried by migratory wildlife. Every other continent, including Antarctica, has been infected by this strain of H5N1 over the past five years, with deaths in the millions. Hundreds of species of birds have been infected, and the virus has evolved to spread more efficiently between mammals. This pattern makes it very difficult to confidently predict how the virus will spread in Australia, but we must be prepared for a widespread and devastating outbreak. What about poultry farms and backyard chooks? There are still no detections of H5N1 in Australian poultry or other livestock, but the risk has increased as confirmed infections rise among resident wild birds. Wild birds can introduce influenza to poultry through direct contact or by contaminating water, feed, footwear and equipment. Backyard owners should prevent contact with wild birds, cover feed and water, avoid untreated surface water, and clean footwear and equipment. Sudden illness or deaths should be reported immediately. Australia’s response now needs to evolve Sadly, the impacts of bird flu on species and ecosystems will play out for decades to come. Australia’s pre-outbreak preparation and coordination has been strong. Federal and state governments established response plans, increased surveillance and prepared the poultry industry before H5N1 arrived. As wild bird infections increase, the poultry industry needs to be supported in implementing biosecurity procedures, and strategic surveillance is needed for both farms and wildlife. Reliable mortality estimates are essential to understand the long-term impacts, and support species to recover. Australia should also assess whether vaccination could protect vulnerable marine mammals before mass deaths begin. We cannot stop wild birds from flying. But we can decide whether this becomes an unmanaged wildlife catastrophe or a closely tracked outbreak, with farms and vulnerable species given timely protection. Please do not touch sick or dead birds or marine mammals. Record the location, take photographs from a safe distance, keep pets away, and report the sighting to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888. analysis.time: Published: August 1, 2026 6:38pm EDT; event ongoing as of publication date.
analysis.location_and_population: Australia (five states), with confirmed detections in South Australia (Robe, Limestone Coast, Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island, Cape Jaffa offshore), and potential inland spread to Monarto, SA. Affected wildlife includes wild seabirds (silver gulls, greater crested terns), seals, sea lions, and endangered Australian sea lions.
analysis.event: A worsening outbreak of H5N1 avian influenza in Australian wildlife, with confirmed local transmission among resident species and potential mass mortality events. Reported by The Conversation as a research-based analysis.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 53 confirmed detections in wild seabirds across five states; 39 confirmed cases in South Australia, including 19 greater crested terns and a silver gull at Robe. Aerial surveillance in SA identified 49 dead and 35 sick greater crested terns (awaiting confirmation). news.content: Australia to Be Dealing Avian Influenza Outbreak for Long Period X/ @1shareShare1 August 4, 2026 Hour: 7:21 am 🔗 Comparte este artículo PDF New detections of the H5N1 strain in South Australia and Victoria have taken the national number of cases to 102. On Tuesday, Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said that Australia could be dealing with the H5N1 strain of avian influenza for a long period of time as the number of confirmed cases surpassed 100. RELATED: Italy Confirms Europe’s First Human Case of H9N2 Avian Flu Authorities have increased surveillance of wild birds following local transmission of the deadly strain among greater crested terns and seagulls. The government is listening to experts on how to prevent the strain from spreading to threatened species and agricultural systems, but that the country could be dealing with the outbreak for a “long period of time.” “We have learnt from overseas experience. We’ve done everything we can, but we cannot stop a very virulent, very contagious disease in this bird flu,” Collins said. Australian Chief Veterinary Officer Beth Cookson said that new confirmed detections of the H5N1 strain in South Australia (SA) and Victoria have taken the national total number of cases to 102, 81 of which have been in SA. Cookson said that there have been no detections in Australia’s agricultural system and the risk to human health remains low. Speaking on ABC radio separately on Tuesday, Environment and Water Minister Murray Watt said that Australia is likely to see more mass mortality events. On Monday, the federal government confirmed the Australian continent’s first mass mortality event from the H5N1 strain in a flock of greater crested terns that were found on an island off the SA coast. teleSUR/ JF Source: Xinhua

analysis.brief_en: Australia is confronting an extended H5N1 avian influenza outbreak in wild birds after the national case count surpassed 100, with 81 cases in South Australia and additional detections in Victoria. The federal government confirmed the continent’s first mass mortality event in greater crested terns off South Australia’s coast, while authorities report no spillover into agricultural systems. Agriculture Minister Julie Collins and Chief Veterinary Officer Beth Cookson emphasized the outbreak’s likely long duration and high contagion, noting that while preventive measures are in place, the disease’s virulence complicates containment. The risk to human health is described as low, and experts are advising on safeguarding threatened species and farm sectors. Environment Minister Murray Watt anticipates further mass mortality events as the situation evolves.

news.source_body_en: Australia is confronting an extended H5N1 avian influenza outbreak in wild birds after the national case count surpassed 100, with 81 cases in South Australia and additional detections in Victoria. The federal government confirmed the continent’s first mass mortality event in greater crested terns off South Australia’s coast, while authorities report no spillover into agricultural systems. Agriculture Minister Julie Collins and Chief Veterinary Officer Beth Cookson emphasized the outbreak’s likely long duration and high contagion, noting that while preventive measures are in place, the disease’s virulence complicates containment. The risk to human health is described as low, and experts are advising on safeguarding threatened species and farm sectors. Environment Minister Murray Watt anticipates further mass mortality events as the situation evolves.

news.title: H5N1 detected in humble seagull threatens to spread bird flu beyond the beach
news.excerpt: Unlike other birds detected with the virus so far in Australia, seagulls travel beyond coastal environments to more urban and inland areas too.
news.rss_summary_html: Unlike other birds detected with the virus so far in Australia, seagulls travel beyond coastal environments to more urban and inland areas too.

news.content: Skip to main content Skip to news navigation, settings and search Explore the ABC More from ABC Close menuABC ABC News ABC iview ABC listen Kids & Students Indigenous Information & Services news iview listen Loading ABC News Just In For You Politics World Business Analysis Sport Lifestyle Entertainment Quizzes More Search News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ABC News News Home Science H5N1 detected in humble seagull threatens to spread bird flu beyond the beach ShareShare article analysis H5N1 detected in humble seagull threatens to spread bird flu beyond the beach By environment reporter Peter de Kruijff ABC Science Topic:Avian Influenza Posted Mon 3 Aug 2026 at 3:53pmMon 3 Aug 2026 at 3:53pm Mon 3 Aug 2026 at 3:53pm Silver gulls are highly resourceful birds that move between shorelines, cities and inland environments. (iNaturalist: Darcy Whittaker, Silver gull, CC BY-NC 4.0) It's hard not to think of Australia's hotel quarantine system during the COVID-19 pandemic while waiting to see what would happen with the animal equivalent, a global bird flu panzootic, on our shores. In the early stages of the COVID response we were given the daily numbers of returning Australians testing positive to the virus. All the while we held our breath waiting to see if it would spread out into the wider community. It's been a similar feeling as migratory birds from Antarctic waters started washing up in mid-June with the H5N1 avian influenza that has swept the globe killing millions of animals. Infected giant petrels and a brown skua, that travel seasonally to chill in the ocean off Australia in winter, were kept in vet clinics as we kept our fingers crossed there would be no local spread. But now the humble seagull getting H5N1, coupled with a mass mortality of greater crested terns, marks a new stage for bird flu's spread in Australia. Until the first seagull was detected with H5 in South Australia last week, the only birds with the virus were terns and those migratory seabirds which stick to the ocean or beaches. But seagulls, the common name for the silver gull species, can move vast distances around the country taking advantage of resources be it nicking chips or hanging out at tips. Potential for long-distance spread Seagulls can be found nearly everywhere in Australia, from beaches to cities, freshwater systems, mountains and landfills. They even pop up in the middle of the country when big rains fill up sites like Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre. This lifestyle gives them the potential to act as a crossover species in spreading the virus to a range of different environments and other bird species. "They're more cosmopolitan in their requirements, [eating at] tips, shopping alleys," Chris Purnell, the wetland and migratory shorebirds manager at Birdlife Australia, told me. "They'll mingle with everything and often parasitise [steal from] other birds and eat their eggs." Seagulls also poo in a lot of places, which is one of the big ways the virus spreads. They spend a lot of time around greater crested terns, which have tested positive to H5N1 in SA and Victoria so far, mixing together in large groups. Both species are coming into their nesting seasons where they can form colonies of thousands. Silver gulls in South Australia nest between June and December with the exact timing varying colony to colony. Silver gulls and greater crested terns often mingle on beaches around Australia. (iNaturalist: Tim, Great crested tern, CC BY 4.0) To borrow a term from the COVID-19 pandemic, those are potential super-spreader events. And they are a real concern when this particular type of H5N1, the clade 2.3.4.4b, wiped out millions of wild and domestic birds and thousands of seals around the world in just a few years, including gulls. The black-headed gull, a close relative of the silver gull, has been the subject of mass die-offs in Europe from this type of H5N1, with an estimated 51,000 adult birds dying in 2023 in Poland. Mass bird deaths are a live concern given what has happened elsewhere in the world and with the first Australian mass mortality of 49 dead greater crested terns over the weekend in SA. Australian Chief Veterinary Officer Beth Cookson said on Monday it had taken a little longer than expected to see a localised spread occurring since the first migratory bird detections. "Now that we have got that localised spread, this is following a fairly predictable curve in terms of the number of infections," she said. "Particularly during a period of year as we might start to see birds start to congregate more. "We know when birds and other animals congregate that's where we get more risk of circulation of the virus and onward spread." H5N1 here to stay Technical advice last week to the federal government puts Australia past the point where the virus may have been eradicated, particularly with a local spread occurring in SA. Skye Fruean, the chief veterinary officer of South Australia, said the disease was here to stay. "Once we started to get that really strong evidence of that transmission between the crested terns, that does change things in terms of our decision making." Loading Dr Fruean told SA Country Hour on Friday that surveillance was still the primary focus but state and federal governments were looking now at what else they should be doing in terms of virus management. That includes discussions around what should trigger a mandatory housing order for free-range chicken operations. "At this point in time it is an option open to jurisdictions," Dr Fruean said. Bringing chickens indoors keeps them away from the potential exposure to water contaminated by wild infected birds and the latter's faeces. That's because chickens are highly susceptible to this strain and more than 100 million have died or been culled in the US since its first outbreak in 2022. But it's still early days yet, with states weighing up the risks and whether chickens need to be locked down. Duck, duck, virus The biggest turning point for different states could be when the virus shows up in water fowl like wild ducks. Ducks are thought to have co-evolved with bird flu viruses like H5 as they can be silent spreaders showing little signs of illness. The virus also spreads rapidly among ducks as it can survive for multiple days within freshwater bodies that ducks both defecate in and eat from. It's not out of the realms of possibility that a bird such as a seagull or a pelican could now be the bridging species that takes the virus from the coast and brings it to ducks. When I rang Dr Purnell on Friday he was visiting Victoria's volcanic lake system, west of Melbourne, where seagulls were starting to gather for nesting. Ducks and other freshwater birds are also highly mobile and move between major water systems. So, the virus has the potential to move big distances and make its way around the country from a single incursion. Past tracking studies of species like ibis and spoonbill, for instance, on the east coast of Australia show a 2,000 kilometre flyway over the Murray Darling Basin. Individual birds were tracked flying all along the system and up to northern Queensland. With the local spread of the virus in SA, there are major areas of concern for initial outbreaks in internationally significant wetlands like the Coorong at the mouth of the Murray River. The Coorong is home to more than 200 bird species, and is a major stopover for millions of migratory shorebirds which start arriving in September from the northern hemisphere each year. They too will be vulnerable to the virus. While we can't predict what exactly will happen from now with the virus's spread, any wishful thinking it wouldn't establish in local birds is past. And as federal agriculture minister Julie Collins said on Monday, we should expect to see an increase in the number of birds getting H5N1 in Australia. "Sadly, we do know that once the H5 bird flu is spreading in wildlife and the natural environment, it is not possible to avoid significant losses, which is what we are starting to see now," she said. "Australians should expect to see more [H5] spread and larger numbers now of wildlife being affected." Anyone who sees a dead or sick bird is asked not to touch it and report it to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888. analysis.time: Published 2026-08-03; event described as occurring in early August 2026 with a time range spanning mid-June to early August 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: South Australia, Victoria, and nationally across Australia; affected populations include silver gulls (seagulls), greater crested terns, migratory seabirds (giant petrels, brown skua), and potentially domestic poultry (chickens).
analysis.event: Detection of H5N1 avian influenza in silver gulls in South Australia, marking a new stage in local spread beyond previously affected migratory seabirds and terns; reported by ABC News and Australian Chief Veterinary Officer Beth Cookson; event is confirmed and ongoing.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 49 greater crested terns found dead in South Australia; potential for widespread spread due to silver gull mobility and congregation with other bird species; risk of onward spread to domestic poultry (e.g., chickens) and freshwater birds (e.g., ducks); H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b previously caused mass die-offs globally including gulls and seals.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Australian and South Australian authorities monitoring and investigating; surveillance ongoing; discussions about mandatory housing orders for free-range poultry; no human cases reported in supplied evidence; virus considered here to stay; unresolved questions about future spread to waterfowl and inland wetlands.

analysis.brief_en: Australia has entered a new phase of H5N1 avian influenza spread after the virus was detected in silver gulls in South Australia, expanding beyond previously affected migratory seabirds and terns. The clade 2.3.4.4b strain, which has caused mass die-offs globally, now threatens to move inland via highly mobile gulls that frequent beaches, cities, landfills, and wetlands. Authorities report 49 dead greater crested terns in South Australia and warn that congregation events among gulls and terns could act as super-spreader events. While no human cases are reported, officials are weighing measures such as housing orders for free-range poultry as they assess risks to domestic birds and internationally significant wetlands like the Coorong, a critical stopover for millions of migratory shorebirds.

Authorities report 49 dead greater crested terns in South Australia and warn that congregation events among gulls and terns could act as super-spreader events. While no human cases are reported, officials are weighing measures such as housing orders for free-range poultry as they assess risks to domestic birds and internationally significant wetlands like the Coorong, a critical stopover for millions of migratory shorebirds.

analysis_en.time: Published 2026-08-03; event described as occurring in early August 2026 with a time range spanning mid-June to early August 2026.
analysis_en.location_and_population: South Australia, Victoria, and nationally across Australia; affected populations include silver gulls (seagulls), greater crested terns, migratory seabirds (giant petrels, brown skua), and potentially domestic poultry (chickens).
analysis_en.event: Detection of H5N1 avian influenza in silver gulls in South Australia, marking a new stage in local spread beyond previously affected migratory seabirds and terns; reported by ABC News and Australian Chief Veterinary Officer Beth Cookson; event is confirmed and ongoing.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: 49 greater crested terns found dead in South Australia; potential for widespread spread due to silver gull mobility and congregation with other bird species; risk of onward spread to domestic poultry (e.g., chickens) and freshwater birds (e.g., ducks); H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b previously caused mass die-offs globally including gulls and seals.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: Australian and South Australian authorities monitoring and investigating; surveillance ongoing; discussions about mandatory housing orders for free-range poultry; no human cases reported in supplied evidence; virus considered here to stay; unresolved questions about future spread to waterfowl and inland wetlands.

news.title_zh: 在不起眼的海鸥身上检测到 H5N1 禽流感有可能将禽流感传播到海滩以外
news.source_body_en: Australia has entered a new phase of H5N1 avian influenza spread after the virus was detected in silver gulls in South Australia, expanding beyond previously affected migratory seabirds and terns. The clade 2.3.4.4b strain, which has caused mass die-offs globally, now threatens to move inland via highly mobile gulls that frequent beaches, cities, landfills, and wetlands. Authorities report 49 dead greater crested terns in South Australia and warn that congregation events among gulls and terns could act as super-spreader events. While no human cases are reported, officials are weighing measures such as housing orders for free-range poultry as they assess risks to domestic birds and internationally significant wetlands like the Coorong, a critical stopover for millions of migratory shorebirds.

news.content: Open accessibility guideSkip to sections navigationSkip to contentSkip to footer Log in Our network Log in Expand navigation menuSearch Advertisement EnvironmentConservationBird flu ‘Just the beginning’: First mass deaths from H5N1 bird flu confirmed Nick O'Malley and Brittany Busch Updated August 3, 2026 — 5:36pm,first published 2:37pm Save Log in, register or subscribe to save articles for later. You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share AAA 22View all comments Add us as a preferred source on Google Listen to this article 6 min Advertisement Australians should expect to witness mass wildlife deaths after bird flu was found to have become established on the mainland, as the federal government confirmed dozens of greater crested terns had tested positive for the deadly H5N1 variant that has killed more than 300 million animals around the world. A seagull and the crested terns were found in Robe and at Baudin Rocks respectively, off the southern South Australia coast. An Australian silver gull has tested positive for bird flu. Ken Irwin As the poultry industry braces for stock infections, rangers across the country survey water mammals such as seals and endangered sea lions - known to be susceptible - for the signs, while in the nation’s cities seagulls, possums and other scavenging animals could spread of the virus, exemplifying the breadth of threat the virus poses. “Sadly, we do know that once the H5 bird flu is spreading in wildlife, and the natural environment, it is not possible to avoid significant losses – which is what we are starting to see now,” Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said at a press conference on Monday. “Australians should expect to see more spread and larger numbers now of wildlife being affected.” Environment Minister Murray Watt said the mass deaths in South Australia were “just the beginning” in what is likely to be a “long and difficult journey”. While the risk to human health remains low, an outbreak of a different strain in 2024 led to about 2 million chickens being killed, causing egg shortages. Collins said Australia had improved biosecurity preparations to protect the industry, having learned from the impact of the disease around the world. Advertisement From our partners Advertisement Kate Millar, chief executive of Australia’s largest bird conservation group, Bird Life Australia, likened the mass deaths over the weekend to the moment bird flu first hit South America in 2022. Within months the disease had spread 6000 kilometres along the continent’s coasts, killing millions of birds, as well as seals, otters, dolphins and porpoises. Invasive Species Council chief executive Jack Gough warned the impending disaster would be confronting for the public, likening the onset of bird flu to the animal deaths from the South Australian algal bloom and the Black Summer bushfires. Birdlife Australia’s Dr Michael MacDonald said it was not yet clear what impact bird flu on some beloved species, such as the brush turkey, a macropod with limited range outside this country.Steven Siewert “It’s not going to be theoretical. People are going to confront this. There has been complacency around environmental issues, particularly in our federal politics over the last few years, outside of the climate wars,” Gough said. “But as people start to deal with the grief and reality of mass wildlife deaths, the politicians that get out ahead of it with a good story to tell about funding resilience are going to weather that public shift in sentiment a lot better.” Birdlife Australia head of science Michael MacDonald worked with the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds in the UK when bird flu hit there, and recalled a sense of loss and helplessness when witnessing colonies of seabirds collapse in Wales. All we can do is try to protect the animals from other pressures,” he said. An estimated 13,000 seal pups were killed by the virus on Australia’s sub-Antarctic Heard Island territory, more than three-quarters of new births on the island, before it was carried to the mainland, likely by a large pelagic bird such as a petrel. The disease is now likely to be spread by scavenging birds and mammals, such as common silver gulls – what many would recognise as seagulls – as well as cats and foxes. People have been warned not to approach or touch birds that show signs of bird flu. Symptoms include being unable to stand, walk or fly properly, breathing difficulties, and mass deaths in one area. Bird Life Australia said the onset of the virus strengthened the advice against feeding wild birds such as seagulls and magpies, and chief vet Beth Cookson also said authorities would call on Australians not to “encourage situations where there might be greater aggregations of wild birds. That’s certainly one context where the disease could spread further”. Professor John Woinarski, one of Australia’s leading Australian biologists, said heavy monsoons that have seen an inland sea formed in parts of central Australia could also see the disease spread rapidly inland. “There’s bound to be silver gulls and pelicans and ibis and waterfowl flying into inland Australia and the Murray River system and spreading the infection very rapidly and very extensively, and with dire consequences,” he said. He also warned the disease was likely to hit mammals in Australia, such as Tasmanian devils, quolls and perhaps even platypuses. He said the disease had not yet caused known extinctions around the world, but had driven many animals close to the brink. In cities, species such as possums, which are known to scavenge on dead animals, were likely to be hit alongside all birds. The Albanese government has committed $113 million to prepare a rapid response, which may involve quarantining farms and restricting transport between locations, as well as ramping up efforts to reduce the numbers of feral cats, foxes and pigs. Gough said this was critical not just because these animals preyed upon birds and eggs, but because they can carry the disease and damage critical habitats. “We’re about to have ... big breeding events [in Spring], and we want the next two seasons of breeding events to be as good as we can possibly make them, because we’re going to have these waves of bird flu hitting,” Gough said. “It’s basically a numbers game for wildlife now.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment. Professor John Woinarski, one of Australia’s leading Australian biologists, said heavy monsoons that have seen an inland sea formed in parts of central Australia could also see the disease spread rapidly inland. “There’s bound to be silver gulls and pelicans and ibis and waterfowl flying into inland Australia and the Murray River system and spreading the infection very rapidly and very extensively, and with dire consequences,” he said. He also warned the disease was likely to hit mammals in Australia, such as Tasmanian devils, quolls and perhaps even platypuses. He said the disease had not yet caused known extinctions around the world, but had driven many animals close to the brink. In cities, species such as possums, which are known to scavenge on dead animals, were likely to be hit alongside all birds. The Albanese government has committed $113 million to prepare a rapid response, which may involve quarantining farms and restricting transport between locations, as well as ramping up efforts to reduce the numbers of feral cats, foxes and pigs. Gough said this was critical not just because these animals preyed upon birds and eggs, but because they can carry the disease and damage critical habitats. “We’re about to have ... big breeding events [in Spring], and we want the next two seasons of breeding events to be as good as we can possibly make them, because we’re going to have these waves of bird flu hitting,” Gough said. “It’s basically a numbers game for wildlife now.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment. analysis.location_and_population: Southern South Australia coastal sites (Robe and Baudin Rocks) and sub-Antarctic Heard Island territory; broader Australian mainland at risk; wildlife populations including greater crested terns, silver gulls, seals, sea lions, possums, Tasmanian devils, quolls, platypuses, and waterfowl (N5, N6, N29, N37, N39).
analysis.event: Australian authorities confirmed local transmission of H5N1 avian influenza in wildlife, marking a significant escalation; described as 'just the beginning' of mass wildlife deaths; federal ministers and conservation leaders warn of extensive spread and significant losses; public advised not to approach or touch sick birds (N4, N8, N9, N26, N31).

analysis.brief_en: Australia has confirmed local transmission of H5N1 avian influenza in wildlife, with mass deaths already reported among greater crested terns and an estimated 13,000 seal pups on sub-Antarctic Heard Island. Federal ministers warn the outbreak is ‘just the beginning,’ signaling extensive spread across mainland bird and mammal populations. Conservation groups liken the unfolding crisis to earlier devastation in South America, where millions of birds and marine mammals perished within months. The government has pledged AUD 113 million for rapid-response measures, including farm quarantines and feral animal control, while urging the public not to feed wild birds or approach sick animals. Scientists caution that heavy inland rains could accelerate spread via waterfowl, with dire consequences for species such as Tasmanian devils and platypuses.

StratNews Global World News Australia China Watch Indo-Pacific Asia Africa Europe North America South America West Asia Russia Neighbours Bhutan China Nepal Pakistan Afghanistan Sri Lanka Myanmar Maldives Videos Documentaries Support Us Home Australia Australia Confirms First Mass Seabird Deaths Linked To H5N1 Bird Flu Australia Confirms First Mass Seabird Deaths Linked To H5N1 Bird Flu By Team StratNews - August 3, 2026 Select Preferred on Google News Discover more Death & Tragedy Birds Bird Australia on Monday warned of the potential for a wider spread of the H5N1 bird flu virus after the country’s first mass seabird die-off claimed around 50 greater crested terns along the coast south of Adelaide. Authorities said there is still no evidence that the virus has reached Australia’s poultry farms, many of which have been under strict biosecurity measures since H5N1 was first detected in the country in June. Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said testing confirmed H5N1 bird flu in a group of 49 dead and 35 sick terns found by helicopter surveillance on rocks off Cape Jaffa, 250 km (155 miles) from Adelaide on Friday. Officials Warn of Wider Wildlife Spread “Australians should expect to see more spread and larger numbers now of wildlife being affected,” she told reporters in Canberra, the capital. “This is the first confirmed case of a mass mortality,” she added. “Once the H5 bird flu is spreading in wildlife and the natural environment, it is not possible to avoid significant losses, which is what we’re starting to see now.” Australia’s tally of 74 confirmed cases is spread as wide as the states of Western Australia and Queensland, though most cases were in South Australia, Collins said. Biosecurity Measures Intensified Australia and New Zealand – which saw its first H5N1 case last month – have spent years bracing for the virus, with steps such as tighter biosecurity at farms, testing of shore birds, vaccinating vulnerable species and war-gaming response plans. The virus has killed hundreds of millions of birds and mammals in recent years, causing billions of dollars in losses to poultry farmers, infecting cattle in the United States and littering beaches with corpses of birds and seals. H5N1 bird flu can infect humans who have contact with infected animals. But the number of cases worldwide is small and officials say the risk to humans is low. news.source_body_en: Australia confirmed its first mass seabird die-off linked to H5N1 avian influenza on August 3, 2026, after testing detected the virus in 49 dead and 35 sick greater crested terns along the coast south of Adelaide. The national tally of 74 confirmed H5N1 cases spans multiple states, though poultry farms remain unaffected. Agriculture Minister Julie Collins warned that wider wildlife spread is likely and that significant losses are expected. Australia has intensified biosecurity measures, including farm safeguards, shore bird testing, and vaccination of vulnerable species, while global risk to humans is assessed as low despite widespread outbreaks in birds and mammals worldwide.

Photograph: Veronica Miller ‘We expected it, but now it’s here’: on the frontline of Australia’s bird flu outbreak, people are distressed As Australia prepares for the H5 bird flu to potentially rip through hundreds of species, residents of the Limestone Coast are already seeing the impacts Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast It has only been three weeks since H5 bird flu was detected on South Australia’s Limestone Coast and already encounters with sick or dead birds are becoming commonplace. Maureen Christie, who lives in the seaside town of Carpenter Rocks, has been observing and protecting birds in the region for decades. She is now witnessing many stricken and suffering. “It’s just awful,” Christie said, who helped establish the Friends of Shorebirds SE more than 20 years ago. “We expected it but, now it’s here, it’s just traumatic.” The state’s south-east is renowned for its bird life, she said, which includes resident hooded plovers and oyster catchers, along with fly-ins from other countries, such as double-banded plovers, red-necked stints, sanderlings and ruddy turnstones. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Locals have been following state government advice to “avoid, record and report”, she said. Christie said many people have been getting in touch by email and phone to relay their own sightings and reports. “Everybody’s feeling distressed, but everybody’s trying to be supportive of one another.” Since the first case in a local Australian seabird – a greater crested tern – was detected in early July, the region has seen dozens more suspected and confirmed cases, including the first confirmed mass mortality event at Baudin Rocks, a group of islets about 8km from the coastal town of Robe. “Robe has a very special and unique environment that the local community knows, uses, celebrates and cares for,” the president of Friends of Little Dip Conservation Park and Robe Coast Care, Roland Wells, said. There’s everything from migratory, coastal and inland birds, wombats, wallabies and echidnas, as well as marine mammals such as sea lions, seals and dolphins. He said people have undertaken conservation work over many decades to support shorebirds, which makes the recent arrival of bird flu “very upsetting”. The situation has escalated considerably over the past week. Council officers from Robe district council have been identifying and reporting sick and deceased birds almost daily, mainly greater crested terns and some silver gulls. Penguins and dolphins among nearly 400 Australian species under threat from bird flu as ‘true extent of disaster’ revealed Read more A spokesperson for South Australia’s primary industries department said crested terns – which make up many of the bird flu cases – “commonly commingle” with other species like cormorants, gulls, grebes, ducks and other tern species. This increases the potential for transmission. “From a conservation perspective, several threatened and priority species have been identified as high risk, including fairy terns,” the spokesperson said. “Marine mammals are also being closely monitored, with Australian sea lions and long-nosed fur seals among the species considered most vulnerable to potential impacts from the virus.” Wildlife carers and clinics – now required to don personal protective equipment and undertake strict cleaning and quarantine measures when dealing with other wild birds injured by cars, in dog and cat attacks or entanglement – have been calling on the state government for support. Mish Simpson, from SKER wildlife veterinary centre, said the clinic was already at capacity before bird flu. But now, more wild birds are being brought in because other vets have stopped accepting them, partly due to the additional requirements and the risk of exposure for other animals. Simpson is concerned there is not enough emphasis on slowing the spread, which would give vets, carers and the community more time to prepare. For example, she said, the dead bodies of infected birds are often being left in the environment, where they pose an infection risk to other wildlife, particularly scavengers. As the federal environment minister, Murray Watt, observed on Monday, the events rapidly unfolding in the south-east, and around Australia, are “the beginning of what is likely to be a long, difficult journey in terms of the impacts on wildlife”. In Victoria, the chief veterinary officer, Dr Graeme Cooke, said recent aerial and ground surveillance near Portland and Nelson has already shown “a clear increase in the number of dead terns along that part of the coast”, consistent with deaths in South Australia. “Last week we talked about individual detections; the first cases of the H5 bird flu in Victoria. We are now seeing a change.” What that means for hundreds of native species and the people who care for them remains uncertain. analysis.time: Published 2026-08-06; event began in early July 2026 with first detection in a local seabird and escalated over the past week.
analysis.location_and_population: South Australia’s Limestone Coast, particularly Pelican Point, Baudin Rocks (8 km from Robe), Carpenter Rocks, and coastal towns including Robe and Portland; affected species include greater crested terns, silver gulls, fairy terns, penguins, dolphins, sea lions, long-nosed fur seals, wombats, wallabies, echidnas, and shorebirds such as hooded plovers and oyster catchers.
analysis.event: Australia’s first confirmed H5 bird flu outbreak in wild seabirds, now spreading among multiple species; confirmed mass mortality event at Baudin Rocks; local communities and wildlife carers report distress and increased sick/dead bird sightings; state government advises 'avoid, record and report'; federal environment minister describes unfolding events as 'the beginning of what is likely to be a long, difficult journey'.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Dozens of suspected and confirmed cases in South Australia; confirmed mass mortality event at Baudin Rocks; increased dead terns reported in Victoria near Portland and Nelson; multiple threatened species identified as high risk including fairy terns; marine mammals (Australian sea lions, long-nosed fur seals) considered most vulnerable; wildlife clinics overwhelmed and at capacity; risk of environmental contamination from uncollected carcasses posing infection risk to scavengers.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: South Australia’s primary industries department monitoring and testing; state government advises public to avoid, record, and report sick or dead birds; wildlife carers and clinics implementing PPE and quarantine measures; calls for greater emphasis on slowing spread; federal and state officials monitoring situation; uncertainty remains about long-term impacts on hundreds of native species and human exposure pathways.

analysis.brief_en: Since early July 2026, Australia has confirmed its first H5 bird flu outbreak in wild seabirds along the Limestone Coast in South Australia, with dozens of suspected and confirmed cases and a confirmed mass mortality event at Baudin Rocks. The outbreak has spread to Victoria, where aerial and ground surveillance near Portland and Nelson shows a clear increase in dead terns. Threatened species such as fairy terns and marine mammals including Australian sea lions and long-nosed fur seals are considered highly vulnerable. Local communities and wildlife carers report widespread distress and increased sightings of sick and dead birds, while wildlife clinics face capacity constraints and implement strict biosecurity measures. Authorities urge the public to avoid, record, and report sick or dead birds, but emphasize that the true extent of the disaster and long-term impacts on hundreds of native species remain uncertain.
analysis.summary_en: Since early July 2026, Australia has confirmed its first H5 bird flu outbreak in wild seabirds along the Limestone Coast in South Australia, with dozens of suspected and confirmed cases and a confirmed mass mortality event at Baudin Rocks. The outbreak has spread to Victoria, where aerial and ground surveillance near Portland and Nelson shows a clear increase in dead terns. Threatened species such as fairy terns and marine mammals including Australian sea lions and long-nosed fur seals are considered highly vulnerable. Local communities and wildlife carers report widespread distress and increased sightings of sick and dead birds, while wildlife clinics face capacity constraints and implement strict biosecurity measures. Authorities urge the public to avoid, record, and report sick or dead birds, but emphasize that the true extent of the disaster and long-term impacts on hundreds of native species remain uncertain.

elements_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: South Australia’s primary industries department monitoring and testing; state government advises public to avoid, record, and report sick or dead birds; wildlife carers and clinics implementing PPE and quarantine measures; calls for greater emphasis on slowing spread; federal and state officials monitoring situation; uncertainty remains about long-term impacts on hundreds of native species and human exposure pathways.

news.title_zh: “我们预料到了,但现在它来了”:在澳大利亚禽流感 暴发 的前线,人们很痛苦 - 《卫报》
news.source_body_en: Since early July 2026, Australia has confirmed its first H5 bird flu outbreak in wild seabirds along the Limestone Coast in South Australia, with dozens of suspected and confirmed cases and a confirmed mass mortality event at Baudin Rocks. The outbreak has spread to Victoria, where aerial and ground surveillance near Portland and Nelson shows a clear increase in dead terns. Threatened species such as fairy terns and marine mammals including Australian sea lions and long-nosed fur seals are considered highly vulnerable. Local communities and wildlife carers report widespread distress and increased sightings of sick and dead birds, while wildlife clinics face capacity constraints and implement strict biosecurity measures. Authorities urge the public to avoid, record, and report sick or dead birds, but emphasize that the true extent of the disaster and long-term impacts on hundreds of native species remain uncertain.
news.content_zh: 自2026年7月初以来,澳大利亚在南澳大利亚石灰岩海岸沿线的野生海鸟中确认了首例H5禽流感死亡率,其中有数十例疑似和确诊病例,并在博丹岩确认了大规模死亡率事件。暴发 已蔓延到维多利亚州,波特兰和尼尔森附近的空中和地面 暴发 显示死亡燕鸥明显增加。受威胁的物种,如仙女燕鸥和海洋哺乳动物,包括澳大利亚海狮和长鼻海狗,被认为是高度脆弱的。当地社区和野生动物护理人员报告称,普遍存在痛苦,病鸟和死鸟的数量有所增加,而野生动物诊所面临能力限制并实施严格的生物安全措施。当局敦促公众避免、记录和报告病鸟或死鸟,但强调灾难的真实程度以及对数百种本地物种的长期影响仍不确定。

CANBERRA: A growing outbreak of H5N1 avian influenza in South Australia (SA) will "almost certainly" spread to an endangered species of sea lion, an expert has warned. Authorities in SA reported that Australia's first suspected case of the highly pathogenic strain in a seagull has been detected on the state's south-east coast. It takes the total number of suspected cases of the strain in SA to 21 in addition to 19 confirmed cases. As of Friday (July 31), the rest of Australia's states and territories had reported 14 confirmed cases of the strain, which was first detected on the mainland in June. Of the 40 confirmed or suspected cases in SA, 33 have been reported since Monday, including four that were detected on Kangaroo Island off the state's south coast. One of the Kangaroo Island cases was detected at Seal Bay, which is home to about five per cent of the global population of the endangered Australian sea lion. Wayne Boardman, a wildlife veterinarian from the University of Adelaide, told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation on Friday that historical events in South America have shown that sea lions and fur seals are particularly susceptible to the strain. Authorities in SA reported that Australia's first suspected case of the highly pathogenic strain in a seagull has been detected on the state's south-east coast.
