As of Friday (July 31), the rest of Australia's states and territories had reported 14 confirmed cases of the strain, which was first detected on the mainland in June. Of the 40 confirmed or suspected cases in SA, 33 have been reported since Monday, including four that were detected on Kangaroo Island off the state's south coast. Photograph: leelakajonkij/Getty Images/iStockphoto View image in fullscreen Little penguins are among numerous species at very high risk from deadly H5N1, a federal government assessment has revealed. Photograph: leelakajonkij/Getty Images/iStockphoto Penguins and dolphins among nearly 400 Australian species under threat from bird flu as ‘true extent of disaster’ revealed Assessment of more than 2,000 native species warns nearly one in five at high risk of deadly H5N1, including parrots, fur seals and quolls Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here Almost 400 native Australian bird and mammal species have been assessed as being at a high risk – or worse – from the deadly H5N1 bird flu virus, a federal government assessment has revealed. Some of Australia’s most beloved animals – including species of penguins, fur seals, quolls, dolphins, more than 300 birds and the Tasmanian devil – are considered at least high risk from the virus, meaning they could suffer “severe reduction in population size or viability” or worse if it reached them. Five species are considered at extreme risk, meaning “unlikely to survive where the virus occurs”. Suspected mass bird flu deaths found in second state as Murray Watt warns ‘this is the beginning’ Read more These are all birds that breed in single islands or groups of islands, such as the endangered Christmas Island frigatebird and the critically endangered herald petrel, which only breeds on Raine Island in the far north of the Great Barrier Reef. More than 80 endangered and critically endangered species are also considered to be facing at least a high risk from an infection, suggesting that the H5N1 strain of bird flu will push them further towards extinction. The federal government released the results of the assessment of more than 2,000 native species, carried out with Charles Darwin University and BirdLife Australia, on Tuesday evening. Nearly one in five have been rated as facing extreme, very high or high risk. View image in fullscreen Australian sea lions, whose populations have declined by 60% in four decades, are at very high risk of H5N1. Photograph: Brad Leue/Alamy Australia’s three resident seals – the Australian fur seal, the New Zealand fur seal and the Australian sea lion – are all considered at very high risk. The Tasmanian devil and the eastern quoll, both assessed as high risk, are the land mammals at greatest threat. The extent of the analysis and the number of species considered at high risk underlines expert fears for the threat to local wildlife. Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter Prof John Woinarski, a leading conservation scientist at Charles Darwin University who helped devise the analysis, said: “This has sketched out a more bleak picture than perhaps we considered previously. “We are going to get major consequences for many species and our bird and mammal diversity is likely to suffer substantial impacts from this disease.” View image in fullscreen Tasmanian devils and eastern quolls are the land mammals at greatest threat. Photograph: Eric J Woehler Prof Hugh Possingham of the University of Queensland, a lead councillor at the Biodiversity Council, said the analysis was “a good first cut” but it should have been released two years ago. “A year ago we needed a priority action list and we should have been taking action then because everyone knew that it was coming,” he said. Kate Millar, the chief executive of BirdLife Australia, said while the list of species at high risk or worse was “long” and “incredibly confronting” it also meant Australia could “prioritise and take action protecting the species most at risk”. Jack Gough, the chief executive of the Invasive Species Council, said the “list of doom” revealed “the true extent of the disaster facing Australian wildlife”. He said it demanded a “serious response” from the government “but instead we have had cuts to on-ground environment programs nationally”. “Almost one in five Australian mammals and birds has been rated by the government as at risk of severe population reductions or even extinction,” he said. “This includes quolls, parrots, seals and pelicans.” View image in fullscreen The critically endangered orange-bellied parrot is among several parrot species at high risk of bird flu. Photograph: Minden Pictures/Alamy The council is among several conservation groups calling for the government to fund a $200m package to scale up on-ground efforts to protect wildlife, including feral animal controls. The government has said it has committed $113m to prepare for bird flu, including $47m “to accelerate protective action” for threatened species and biodiversity. The environment minister, Murray Watt, said the risk analysis had already informed investments to protect captive animal populations, removing feral threats and inoculating against more common diseases. “We have been investing in these types of projects across the country for several years in preparation for a bird flu outbreak, and as a result, our native species are in a better position to withstand the H5 incursion.” Jess Abrahams, national nature campaigner at the Australian Conservation Foundation, said: “Australia is already in the midst of an extinction crisis and we need to be prepared for just how harrowing this could get. “Australians love nature and we all need to be emotionally prepared for the onslaught that could occur and know what to do if they come across a sick, dying or dead animal.” The H5N1 virus has killed millions of birds and mammals since it spread from Europe in 2021 to every continent on the planet. Australia was the final continent to be breached six weeks ago, when infected Antarctic and subantarctic migratory seabirds were found dead and sick in Western Australia and South Australia. The virus has now been confirmed in more than 100 individual birds and air surveillance has recorded the first mass mortality event from the disease, in South Australia. Detections have also been confirmed in Victoria, New South Wales and Queensland. analysis.time: The federal government released the assessment on Tuesday evening, with the virus spreading to Australia six weeks prior and confirmed in more than 100 individual birds and South Australia's first mass mortality event (N1, N28, N29).
analysis.location_and_population: Australia, specifically mentioning Western Australia, South Australia, Victoria, New South Wales, and Queensland, with nearly 400 native bird and mammal species at risk, including penguins, dolphins, fur seals, quolls, and the Tasmanian devil (N1, N3, N12, N22, N24).
analysis.event: A federal government assessment revealed that nearly 400 Australian native species are at high risk from H5N1 bird flu, with five species considered at extreme risk. The assessment was conducted in collaboration with Charles Darwin University and BirdLife Australia (N3, N8, N12, N13, N21).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The assessment identified that almost one in five Australian mammals and birds are at risk of severe population reductions or extinction. Some species, such as the Tasmanian devil and eastern quoll, are at high risk, while five are at extreme risk (N5, N7, N9, N13, N21).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The government has committed $113m to prepare for bird flu, including $47m for protective action for threatened species. However, conservation groups are calling for increased funding, and the government has not yet confirmed the full extent of the outbreak or its impact on wildlife (N24, N25, N23).

analysis.brief_en: A federal government assessment, conducted with Charles Darwin University and BirdLife Australia, has revealed that nearly 400 native Australian bird and mammal species are at high risk from the deadly H5N1 bird flu virus. The assessment, released on Tuesday evening, highlights that almost one in five Australian mammals and birds face severe population reductions or extinction. The virus was confirmed in South Australia six weeks ago, following its spread from Europe in 2021. Five species are considered at extreme risk, including the Tasmanian devil and eastern quoll. The government has allocated $113m to prepare for bird flu, but conservation groups are urging more funding to protect wildlife. The findings underscore the growing threat to Australia's biodiversity and the need for urgent action.

Photograph: imageBROKER/David & Micha Sheldon/Getty Images/imageBROKER RF View image in fullscreen More than 80 dead and dying greater crested terns have been spotted off the South Australian coast in what is a suspected H5N1 bird flu mass mortality event. Photograph: imageBROKER/David & Micha Sheldon/Getty Images/imageBROKER RF First Australian mass mortality event suspected as deadly bird flu virus rapidly escalates among native birds Helicopter surveillance finds dead and dying greater crested terns off South Australian coast as H5 virus spreads Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast More than 80 dead and sick birds seen on rocks off the South Australian coast are suspected to be the first mass mortality event from the deadly H5N1 bird flu virus, only six weeks after the disease arrived in Australia. Authorities reported on Saturday that helicopter surveillance had revealed 49 dead greater crested terns on Baudin Rocks, near Robe, as well as 35 more sick terns. While some of the birds had been collected for testing, South Australia’s chief vet Skye Fruean said it was likely the first mass mortality event from the disease. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email South Australia also reported three suspected positive cases in other greater crested terns, including one inland at Monarto, suggesting the disease has begun moving away from the coast. The Monarto area is home to several poultry farms. Three silver gulls were also suspected positive, SA authorities said, adding to the first silver gull found a few days ago and confirmed positive by the CSIRO earlier on Saturday. Kate Millar, the chief executive of conservation charity BirdLife Australia, called it a “very significant escalation of the bird flu situation in Australia, and a very bleak milestone”. “Sadly, we’re at the beginning of a long and challenging battle and birds and wildlife are going to need all the help they can get,” she said. Jack Gough, the chief executive of the Invasive Species Council, said it now appeared the disease was “starting to take off” and “mirroring the experience in South America of early detections, then rapid increases in numbers and spread leading to mass mortality events in wildlife.” “We are still at the very early stages of this devastating disease spreading, but the possible first mass mortality coming just days after the virus was declared not eradicable indicates how quickly this could escalate,” he said. Fruean said there was “nothing we can do” to stop the spread of the disease, but that surveillance was working. The news came at the end of a significant week in the development of the disease when numbers jumped by 20 in just a few days to the current total of 53. Australia was the last continent to have the unwelcome arrival of a disease that has killed millions of birds and mammals around the world. Victoria this week confirmed its first cases of the virulent strain in a greater crested tern found in Portland, with the state joining Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales and Queensland that have all recorded positive cases. On Saturday, Victorian authorities said samples from five crested terns had been sent to the CSIRO laboratory in Geelong, with preliminary testing suggesting more positive results. Five confirmed cases in birds at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island also raised concerns for the welfare of the area’s Australian sea lions – an endangered species. Tens of thousands of seals have died worldwide from the disease. But it has been the cases among silver gulls that has experts like Sean Dooley, the national affairs adviser at BirdLife Australia, concerned that the spread of the virus has now reached a critical new stage. “When people think of a seagull, they’re almost always thinking of the silver gull,” said Dooley. skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Australian sea lions, an endangered species, are at risk of contracting H5N1 bird flu. Photograph: Brad Leue/Alamy “They’re very common, and primarily they are coastal, but they do come inland and can turn up in Lake Eyre following floods,” said Dooley. Silver gulls are the second Australian native species to catch the disease, after dozens of detections in greater crested terns. But it is the silver gull’s behaviour and habits that have experts concerned because they scavenge from dead or dying animals, meaning they can easily pick up the disease from other sick birds. They also pick detritus from water bodies – lakes and flooded areas included – and these are known to be breeding grounds for the disease. “There is such a large population of silver gulls, and they move into other habitats. They could be the vector that takes bird flu inland,” says Dooley. “They’re also really successful in urban areas and could bring the disease into those bird populations.” Because Australia has a high concentration of unique birds, the susceptibility of many native species isn’t known. But the fears are there is no reason to think they would manage any better than birds overseas. Birds that flock around water have tended to be the hardest hit. Examples include sandwich terns, black-headed gulls and northern gannets in Europe and, in Peru, pelicans. Dooley said the mood at BirdLife Australia this week had been one of “trying to suppress that sinking, gut-churning feeling”. The winter season for birdwatchers along the coast had been one of the best in 10 years, said Dooley, with rare petrels turning up in numbers along the east coast. “Now that has been heavily tinged because probably among those were birds carrying H5N1.” Explore more on these topics Bird flu Wildlife Birds Marine life Animals news Share Reuse this content Most viewed ACLU blasts Trump’s new orders on birthright citizenship, saying they are doomed to fail in court– as it happened US federal judge halts order for Trump to turn over financial records to BBC US law enforcement gave false information in case against woman charged in anti-ICE protest Miss North Carolina USA stripped of title after alleged racist posts resurface Trump again rebukes Jeanine Pirro over reflecting pool ‘vandalism’ case Most viewed Most viewed

analysis.time: The suspected H5N1 bird flu mass mortality event was reported on August 1, 2026, with the first cases identified in Australia six weeks prior. The event escalated rapidly, with numbers jumping by 20 in a few days to reach a total of 53 cases.
analysis.location_and_population: The event occurred off the South Australian coast, specifically near Baudin Rocks, Robe, and the Monarto area, which is home to poultry farms. It involved greater crested terns and silver gulls, with concerns about the spread to Australian sea lions, an endangered species.
analysis.event: A suspected H5N1 bird flu mass mortality event was identified among native birds in Australia, with 49 dead greater crested terns and 35 sick ones found on Baudin Rocks. Three suspected positive cases were also reported in other terns and silver gulls, indicating the virus is spreading inland.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Over 80 dead and dying greater crested terns were reported, with additional suspected positive cases in silver gulls. The virus has spread to multiple regions in Australia, including Victoria, Western Australia, New South Wales, and Queensland. The risk of further spread to other bird species and wildlife, including Australian sea lions, is highlighted due to the virus's potential to affect large populations.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: South Australia’s chief vet, Skye Fruean, stated that there was "nothing we can do" to stop the spread, but surveillance efforts are ongoing. The CSIRO confirmed the first silver gull case, and further testing is being conducted. The situation remains under investigation, with experts expressing concern about the virus's potential to escalate.

analysis.brief_en: A suspected H5N1 bird flu outbreak has been reported in Australia, marking the first mass mortality event among native birds. Over 80 dead and dying greater crested terns were found off the South Australian coast, with 49 confirmed dead and 35 sick. Three other terns and silver gulls were suspected positive, indicating the virus is spreading inland. The Monarto area, home to poultry farms, and Victoria have also reported cases, with the virus now present in multiple regions. South Australia’s chief vet, Skye Fruean, noted the spread is difficult to stop, but surveillance is ongoing. The outbreak has raised concerns about the impact on Australian sea lions and other wildlife, as silver gulls are known to scavenge and spread the virus. Experts warn of the potential for further escalation, mirroring similar outbreaks in South America and Europe. The situation remains under investigation, with no confirmed methods to halt the spread.

analysis_zh.time: 2026 年 8 月 1 日报告了疑似 H5N1 禽流感集体 死亡率 事件,六周前在澳大利亚发现了第一例病例。该事件迅速升级,几天内病例数增加了 20 例,总数达到 53 例。
analysis_zh.location_and_population: 该事件发生在南澳大利亚海岸附近,特别是博丹岩、罗布和家禽养殖场所在地莫纳托地区附近。它涉及更大的凤头燕鸥和银鸥,人们担心病毒会传播到濒危物种澳大利亚海狮。
analysis_zh.event: 澳大利亚本土鸟类中发现疑似 H5N1 禽流感集体 死亡率 事件,博丹岩石上发现 49 只大凤头燕鸥死亡和 35 只患病燕鸥。其他燕鸥和银鸥也报告了三例疑似阳性病例,表明病毒正在内陆传播。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 据报道,有超过 80 只大凤头燕鸥死亡和垂死,银鸥中还有其他疑似阳性病例。该病毒已传播到澳大利亚多个地区,包括维多利亚州、西澳大利亚州、新南威尔士州和昆士兰州。由于该病毒可能影响大量种群,因此凸显了进一步传播到其他鸟类和野生动物(包括澳大利亚海狮)的风险。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 南澳大利亚州首席兽医 Skye Fruean 表示,“我们无能为力”来阻止病毒传播,但 监测 的努力仍在继续。澳大利亚联邦科学与工业研究组织(CSIRO)确认了首例银鸥病例,目前正在进行进一步测试。目前情况仍在调查中,专家对病毒可能升级的可能性表示担忧。

news.content: Open accessibility guideSkip to sections navigationSkip to contentSkip to footer Log in Our network Log in Expand navigation menuSearch Advertisement EnvironmentConservationBird flu ‘List of doom’: Bird flu puts one in five Australian bird and mammal species at risk Nick O'Malley August 5, 2026 — 5:00am Save Log in, register or subscribe to save articles for later. You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share AAA Add us as a preferred source on Google Listen to this article 5 min Advertisement Almost one in five Australian bird and mammal species is at high, very high or extreme risk from the bird flu virus now spreading in Australia, according to data published on the federal environment department’s website on Tuesday evening. Five bird species are assessed as being at extreme risk, meaning that they cannot survive where the virus occurs. They include the Christmas Island frigate bird, the Herald petrel, Houtman albatross, imperial shag on Heard Island and imperial shag on Macquarie Island. Christmas Island frigate birds are among the species at extreme risk.AP The highest-risk marine mammals are the sea lion, fur seal and elephant seal, and the highest risk land mammals are the Tasmanian devil and eastern quoll. Eight species of dolphin are at risk and one, the common dolphin, is at very high risk. The risk category of each animal has been calculated by assessing both the susceptibility of the animal to the disease and the animal’s conservation status. Animals with limited ranges or those that congregate in habitats known to be prone to the transmission of the H5N1 virus – such as colonies of waterbirds – are considered to be at higher risk. Livestock Animal Health Bird flu vaccine for dairy herds urged as virus spreads Farm Progress America: Disease experts say vaccinating cattle could be the most important step to stop H5N1's advance across US farms. April 17, 2026 The bird flu crisis that started in poultry barns three years ago has evolved into a serious dairy problem, and some disease experts now say it's time to start vaccinating cattle. Dr. Gregory Gray from the University of Texas Medical Branch recently argued in the Journal of Infectious Diseases that vaccinating dairy herds may be the single most important step America can take to get ahead of H5N1 avian influenza. The numbers tell a concerning story. Since the virus jumped into dairy cattle in March 2024, more than 1,000 herds across at least 19 states have been infected. The dairy sector alone has taken a $4 billion hit, part of an estimated $14 billion total economic impact from the outbreak that's killed over 190 million birds since 2022. What worries Dr. Gray most is what happens next. Every infection in a mammal gives the virus another chance to adapt. He describes dairy cattle as a potential training ground for H5N1 to learn how to live in mammals, which increases the risk to humans. The CDC has already tallied 71 human cases with two deaths, mostly among farm workers. Related:USDA restores prevented planting buy-up option for crop insurance The good news? Vaccination could work. Studies show infected cows develop strong immunity lasting a year or longer, and early vaccine trials are producing promising results. Several candidates are currently in USDA field trials, though none are approved yet. Dr. Gray's message is clear: the longer we wait, the harder this gets. news.content_title: Anadolu Ajansı
news.content: World Asia - Pacific Australia confirms 1st mass mortality of wildlife from bird flu Federal Agriculture Minister says risk to human health remains low Saadet Gokce 03 August 2026 • Update : 03 August 2026 İSTANBUL Australia has confirmed its first mass wildlife mass mortality linked to the deadly H5 bird flu, with greater crested terns found on Baudin Rocks, an island off South Australia's southeast coast, local media reported Monday. Dead and sick birds were detected on Friday during aerial surveillance on Baudin Rocks, about 5 kilometers (3 miles) south of Cape Jaffa. Samples collected from the site later tested positive for H5 avian influenza, according to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC). Australia, which remained the only continent free of the deadly virus until June 14, had since only detected bird flu in migratory subantarctic seabirds, mostly giant petrels, found on the coasts of South Australian, Western Australia and New South Wales. The country has recorded 74 confirmed cases of the virus so far, including 54 in South Australia, 10 in Western Australia, seven in Victoria, two in New South Wales, and one in Queensland. Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said the mass mortality was expected. "Sadly, we do know that once the H5 bird flu is spreading in wildlife and the natural environment, it is not possible to avoid significant losses, which is what we're starting to see now." Collins added that there was no evidence of the bird flu in poultry or agricultural systems and the risk to human health remained low. "We have invested and worked really closely with our agriculture, particularly our poultry sector, in terms of improved and increasing biosecurity to do everything we can do to keep it out of our agriculture system,” she said. "But you do tend to see spillover impacts across the globe when it comes to the H5." Collins said Australians could expect to see bird flu continue to spread, with larger numbers of wildlife affected. news.content_original: World Asia - Pacific Australia confirms 1st mass mortality of wildlife from bird flu Federal Agriculture Minister says risk to human health remains low Saadet Gokce 03 August 2026 • Update : 03 August 2026 İSTANBUL Australia has confirmed its first mass wildlife mass mortality linked to the deadly H5 bird flu, with greater crested terns found on Baudin Rocks, an island off South Australia's southeast coast, local media reported Monday. Dead and sick birds were detected on Friday during aerial surveillance on Baudin Rocks, about 5 kilometers (3 miles) south of Cape Jaffa. Samples collected from the site later tested positive for H5 avian influenza, according to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC). Australia, which remained the only continent free of the deadly virus until June 14, had since only detected bird flu in migratory subantarctic seabirds, mostly giant petrels, found on the coasts of South Australian, Western Australia and New South Wales. The country has recorded 74 confirmed cases of the virus so far, including 54 in South Australia, 10 in Western Australia, seven in Victoria, two in New South Wales, and one in Queensland. Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said the mass mortality was expected. "Sadly, we do know that once the H5 bird flu is spreading in wildlife and the natural environment, it is not possible to avoid significant losses, which is what we're starting to see now." Collins added that there was no evidence of the bird flu in poultry or agricultural systems and the risk to human health remained low. "We have invested and worked really closely with our agriculture, particularly our poultry sector, in terms of improved and increasing biosecurity to do everything we can do to keep it out of our agriculture system,” she said. "But you do tend to see spillover impacts across the globe when it comes to the H5." Collins said Australians could expect to see bird flu continue to spread, with larger numbers of wildlife affected. "The reality is you can't stop native and wild birds flying around, and you can't stop wild animals moving around, and that will mean more mass mortality events like the one we have now seen," Federal Environment Minister Murray Watt also said, adding that this is the beginning of "what is likely to be a long, difficult journey in terms of the impacts on wildlife." He said the national management plan for H5 bird flu had been activated, with an extra $24 million from state and federal governments. Australia: Which bird species usually carry avian influenza Deadly bird flu strain in Australia: Which bird species usually carry avian influenza TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 01, 2026, 11:42 IST Comments Share AA +Text Size Small Medium Large In June 2026, Australia confirmed its first-ever detections of high pathogenicity H5 bird flu in wild seabirds, and since then the numbers have kept climbing.As of Aug 1, authorities have confirmed 53 cases of H5 bird flu in wild seabirds across the country, according to the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry. “Testing at CSIRO’s Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness (ACDP) has returned one positive result in a silver gull found at Robe in South Australia. There have now been 53 confirmed or presumed positive detections of H5 bird flu in Australia. This is the first confirmed detection in a silver gull in Australia. There remain no detections in poultry or in our agricultural production system. The risk to human health remains low,” the DAFF said on Aug 1. How it actually got here Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Julie Collins told a news conference that transmission had occurred between greater crested terns in South Australia state.The first confirmed case was a brown skua found sick, and later dead, at Cape Le Grand National Park near Esperance in Western Australia. Not long after, a giant petrel in the same area tested positive too. From there, the virus has kept showing up in new spots and new birds, with confirmed cases now spanning Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales, and Queensland. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like I Added This High‐Risk Biotech To My Watchlist [See my reasoning]VolitionRx Learn More Undo The birds carrying it So which species are actually involved here? Mostly seabirds, and that pattern's held steady since the first case. Terns have been especially hard hit, greater crested terns have turned up positive in multiple locations across South Australia, including Cape Jaffa, Southend, and Port MacDonnell, according to Animal Health Australia. Petrels are another recurring name on the list, with a dead petrel on Moreton Island marking Queensland's first confirmed case. Skuas, like the very first bird that tested positive back in June, are also considered a species of concern.More broadly, wild waterbirds and seabirds are the ones epidemiologists watch most closely with any bird flu strain, because they're the natural hosts for lower pathogenicity versions of the virus and can carry it without showing obvious signs of illness. Migratory birds specifically tend to be the ones that introduce a new strain into a previously unaffected region, simply because of how far and how often they travel. Why this particular strain worries people H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, the strain now confirmed in Australia, is the same one that's caused mass mortality events in wild birds and even mammals like seals across other continents over the past few years. It's part of what's being called the largest and most widespread avian influenza outbreak ever recorded.Australia's Centre for Disease Control has been clear that human infections from bird flu remain rare, and person-to-person spread is rarer still, with the last confirmed case of that happening overseas dating back to 2016. The country did report one human H5N1 infection back in 2024, though that person had picked it up while travelling abroad and made a full recovery. There haven't been any human cases linked to this newer strain circulating since June. Australia: Which bird species usually carry avian influenza Deadly bird flu strain in Australia: Which bird species usually carry avian influenza TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 01, 2026, 11:42 IST Comments Share AA +Text Size Small Medium Large In June 2026, Australia confirmed its first-ever detections of high pathogenicity H5 bird flu in wild seabirds, and since then the numbers have kept climbing.As of Aug 1, authorities have confirmed 53 cases of H5 bird flu in wild seabirds across the country, according to the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry. “Testing at CSIRO’s Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness (ACDP) has returned one positive result in a silver gull found at Robe in South Australia. There have now been 53 confirmed or presumed positive detections of H5 bird flu in Australia. This is the first confirmed detection in a silver gull in Australia. There remain no detections in poultry or in our agricultural production system. The risk to human health remains low,” the DAFF said on Aug 1. How it actually got here Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Julie Collins told a news conference that transmission had occurred between greater crested terns in South Australia state.The first confirmed case was a brown skua found sick, and later dead, at Cape Le Grand National Park near Esperance in Western Australia. Not long after, a giant petrel in the same area tested positive too. From there, the virus has kept showing up in new spots and new birds, with confirmed cases now spanning Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales, and Queensland. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like I Added This High‐Risk Biotech To My Watchlist [See my reasoning]VolitionRx Learn More Undo The birds carrying it So which species are actually involved here? Mostly seabirds, and that pattern's held steady since the first case. Terns have been especially hard hit, greater crested terns have turned up positive in multiple locations across South Australia, including Cape Jaffa, Southend, and Port MacDonnell, according to Animal Health Australia. Petrels are another recurring name on the list, with a dead petrel on Moreton Island marking Queensland's first confirmed case. Skuas, like the very first bird that tested positive back in June, are also considered a species of concern.More broadly, wild waterbirds and seabirds are the ones epidemiologists watch most closely with any bird flu strain, because they're the natural hosts for lower pathogenicity versions of the virus and can carry it without showing obvious signs of illness. Migratory birds specifically tend to be the ones that introduce a new strain into a previously unaffected region, simply because of how far and how often they travel. Why this particular strain worries people H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, the strain now confirmed in Australia, is the same one that's caused mass mortality events in wild birds and even mammals like seals across other continents over the past few years. It's part of what's being called the largest and most widespread avian influenza outbreak ever recorded.Australia's Centre for Disease Control has been clear that human infections from bird flu remain rare, and person-to-person spread is rarer still, with the last confirmed case of that happening overseas dating back to 2016. The country did report one human H5N1 infection back in 2024, though that person had picked it up while travelling abroad and made a full recovery. There haven't been any human cases linked to this newer strain circulating since June. news.source_body_en: Australia has confirmed 53 cases of high pathogenicity H5 bird flu in wild seabirds as of August 1, 2026. The first detection was a brown skua found sick and later dead at Cape Le Grand National Park in Western Australia. Since then, the virus has spread to other regions, including South Australia, New South Wales, and Queensland, with confirmed cases in greater crested terns, petrels, and skuas. Testing at CSIRO’s Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness (ACDP) found one positive result in a silver gull at Robe in South Australia. Notably, there have been no detections in poultry or agricultural systems, and the risk to human health remains low. The outbreak is part of a larger global avian influenza event, with H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b being the strain identified. Human infections from bird flu are rare, and person-to-person spread is even rarer, with the last confirmed case overseas dating back to 2016. Australia's Centre for Disease Control has emphasized that no human cases linked to this newer strain have been reported since June 2026.

news.content: Toggle search form Search for: Toggle navigation Oklahoma Farm Report Home Listen to Us Markets Ag News Ag News Agri-Innovations Blue Green Gazette Weather Calendar Auctions Daily Emails Daily Emails Archives Subscribe to Daily Email About Us About Us Our Team Oklahoma Farm Report Radio Affiliates Beef Buzz Contact Contact Us Advertise With Us Email Us a Story/Idea/Content Congressman Brecheen August Town Halls – Oklahoma – 8/24-26, 2026 National FFA Reaches Record 1.05 Million Student Members Across Nearly 9,600 Chapters Aug 04 Bird Flu on the Move: Understanding Seasonal HPAI Risk in the Mississippi Flyway Jada Thompson, Associate Professor, Department of Agricultural Economics and Agribusiness Ryan Loy, Assistant Professor and Extension Economist, Department of Agricultural Economics and Agribusiness Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), commonly called bird flu refers to the H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b strain of avian influenza, which was detected in the United States in 2022. The term “highly pathogenic” refers to the virus’s ability to spread quickly and destructively, killing more than 75% of birds it infects (World Organisation for Animal Health, 2026). Because the virus is so deadly in commercial poultry, best practice requires the depopulation of flocks in which the disease is detected. Primarily, this is the humane response, as the entire flock will perish if given enough time. Depopulation also stops the reproduction of the virus, protecting farmers, consumers, and the public. Additionally, it allows farmers to minimize down time, returning farms to production as soon as possible, after appropriate cleaning and disinfection. Though necessary, these population losses lead to economic consequences which extend well beyond just individual farms, contributing significantly to elevated egg prices (Mitchell et al., 2024). Bird Flu in the Flyway The U.S. poultry industry encountered H5N2 HPAI in 2014, which was mostly spread house-to-house through contaminated materials, trucks, and laborers. This prompted sweeping changes in biosecurity culture that still exist today. These changes, along with a single warm summer, helped to end the outbreak by June 2015. Since the 2022 introduction of a host-adapted H5N1 virus, poultry growers in the Mississippi Flyway have faced increased disease risk, despite the wide adoption of these enhanced biosecurity measures. This most recent outbreak has spread instead by external introduction, rather than in the same fashion as in 2014. In this case, “host-adapted” refers to the virus’s ability to persist in wild bird populations. Whereas previous HPAI events ravaged both poultry and wild birds, the current H5N1 2.3.4.4b classification is less likely to kill wild bird species (Patyk et al., 2023; Thompson et al., 2025). This means that waterfowl can become infected and still survive migration, spreading the disease across the flyway. What is the Mississippi flyway? Discover more Farm Farms & Ranches Agriculture & Forestry Migratory birds follow predictable migratory corridors, called flyways. The Mississippi flyway is an economically important flyway, covering parts of more than fifteen states and two Canadian provinces which include commercial broiler, turkey, and egg production. Migratory fowl spend the warm summer months in the breeding grounds of the northern Midwest, leaving in the fall to ride cold fronts south towards over-wintering habitat in the Gulf States. For southern states like Arkansas and Louisiana, the regularity of this migration is a large source of off-farm income, as waterfowl hunters flock to the Mississippi Delta. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service estimates that migratory bird hunters in Arkansas spend nearly $300 million annually on lodging, equipment, food, and transportation, over the state’s 72-day waterfowl season (U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, 2022). Birds begin moving north again in the spring, often returning to the same breeding region year after year. Aside from its incredible biodiversity during migrations, the wetland habitat along the Mississippi River acts as a natural flood barrier year-round, holding surplus water as it drains towards the river. Examining the geographic distribution of HPAI detections over time reveals a clear seasonal pattern that mirrors waterfowl migration. Figure 1 shows the number of detections, by county, for each month over the course of the outbreak. During the summer months, detections are sparse and concentrated in the northern reaches of the flyway, where birds spend the breeding season. As fall migration begins, HPAI’s geographic footprint expands southward, spanning nearly the entire flyway from October through May. Figure 1: Mississippi Flyway HPAI Detections by Month, 2022-2025, with fitted latitudinal mean and IQR What does this mean? Understanding seasonality affords producers a predictable window each year to prepare before peak exposure periods arrive. Before Peak Season Inspect and repair perimeter fencing, netting, and housing gaps that could allow wildlife to access farm premises. Evaluate water and feed delivery systems to ensure they too are isolated from outside contact. Review all available extension publications, updating biosecurity protocols where necessary while maintaining coverage status with livestock indemnity programs. Conduct training and review these protocols with all farm workers and establish relationships with your veterinarian and state animal health officials before an emergency arises. Budget for increased biosecurity expenditures and most importantly, ensure you have a financial emergency plan, should you face depopulation. During Peak Season Vigilantly adhere to enhanced biosecurity protocols without exception. Monitor flocks closely for behavioral changes, decreased feed and water consumption, or sudden mortality. Limit all non-essential personnel traffic and enforce strict entry and exit biosecurity for all visitors and vehicles. Report any unusual mortality to your veterinarian or the USDA at 1-866-536-7593. Year-Round Stay current with USDA APHIS detection reports to understand active disease pressure in your region. Participate in state and federal livestock indemnity programs and know your coverage. The Big Picture A host-adapted virus in a migratory population means recurring seasonal risk for the foreseeable future. However, that seasonality also gives producers, researchers, and communities time to plan ahead. Understanding when and where the disease is likely to appear turns an unpredictable force into a manageable calendar of preparation and vigilance. Extension agents and agricultural educators can use these materials to help producers understand local risk windows and connect with available resources. Community preparedness, which begins at the farm level, remains the most effective tool available against this disease. analysis.location_and_population: Mississippi Flyway, covering parts of more than fifteen U.S. states and two Canadian provinces; includes commercial broiler, turkey, and egg production regions.
analysis.event: Guidance article on seasonal risk of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b in the Mississippi Flyway, including historical outbreak context and recommended biosecurity measures.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Economic impact noted via elevated egg prices linked to depopulation; seasonal pattern of HPAI detections mirrors waterfowl migration, with sparse summer detections and broader geographic spread during fall-to-spring migration; no case or death counts reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Recommended actions include pre-peak season biosecurity inspections, financial planning for depopulation, vigilant monitoring during peak season, and year-round engagement with USDA APHIS detection reports; uncertainty acknowledged regarding recurring seasonal risk due to host-adapted virus in migratory wild birds.

analysis.brief_en: A seasonal risk briefing on highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b in the Mississippi Flyway warns producers of recurring outbreaks tied to waterfowl migration. The virus, first detected in U.S. poultry in 2022, spreads via wild birds that survive infection and migrate, expanding geographic detections from October through May. While summer detections are sparse, fall-to-spring migration drives broader spread across the flyway, which spans over fifteen U.S. states and two Canadian provinces and supports major commercial poultry sectors. Economic losses from depopulation contribute to elevated egg prices, underscoring the need for pre-peak biosecurity upgrades, financial contingency planning, and vigilant flock monitoring. Authored by agricultural economists, the guidance emphasizes community preparedness and adherence to USDA reporting and indemnity programs to mitigate recurring seasonal risk.

The virus, first detected in U.S. poultry in 2022, spreads via wild birds that survive infection and migrate, expanding geographic detections from October through May. While summer detections are sparse, fall-to-spring migration drives broader spread across the flyway, which spans over fifteen U.S. states and two Canadian provinces and supports major commercial poultry sectors. Economic losses from depopulation contribute to elevated egg prices, underscoring the need for pre-peak biosecurity upgrades, financial contingency planning, and vigilant flock monitoring. Authored by agricultural economists, the guidance emphasizes community preparedness and adherence to USDA reporting and indemnity programs to mitigate recurring seasonal risk.

news.source_body_en: A seasonal risk briefing on highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b in the Mississippi Flyway warns producers of recurring outbreaks tied to waterfowl migration. The virus, first detected in U.S. poultry in 2022, spreads via wild birds that survive infection and migrate, expanding geographic detections from October through May. While summer detections are sparse, fall-to-spring migration drives broader spread across the flyway, which spans over fifteen U.S. states and two Canadian provinces and supports major commercial poultry sectors. Economic losses from depopulation contribute to elevated egg prices, underscoring the need for pre-peak biosecurity upgrades, financial contingency planning, and vigilant flock monitoring. Authored by agricultural economists, the guidance emphasizes community preparedness and adherence to USDA reporting and indemnity programs to mitigate recurring seasonal risk.

What can Australia do differently? Published: August 4, 2026 4:05pm EDT •Updated: August 4, 2026 10:12pm EDT Australia is now confronting an outbreak of a deadly bird flu strain. As of Monday, the highly pathogenic H5N1 virus had been detected in 78 wild birds across mainland Australia. Until now, there had been no evidence of a large-scale outbreak. But authorities have confirmed the first instance of mass death caused by H5N1 among dozens of greater crested terns off South Australia’s south-east coast. They are also conducting further testing on a cluster of sick and dead terns in south-west Victoria. As H5N1 spreads across the country, researchers, wildlife managers and the broader public are increasingly concerned about the risks it may pose beyond birds. Recent outbreaks have threatened aquatic mammals, including southern otters, dolphins and porpoises. H5N1 has also decimated pinniped populations around the globe, including in South America. Pinnipeds are marine mammals that live in the sea and form colonies but spend extended periods on land, such as sea lions, fur seals and elephant seals. As the risk of a broader outbreak rises, Australia must protect its wildlife by drawing on lessons from other continents already battling bird flu. Looking to South America H5N1 poses an urgent threat to wildlife worldwide. Since 2021, this fatal strain of bird flu has spread to every continent and infected poultry flocks, dairy cattle, wild birds and a growing range of wild mammals. In June, it finally reached Australia, first detected in a sick brown skua. This strain has been particularly devastating in South America. In late 2022, H5N1 spread rapidly from infected seabirds into pinniped colonies. At least 30,000 South American sea lions died in Peru, Chile, Argentina, Uruguay and Brazil during the subsequent outbreak. In some areas, major breeding colonies lost up to one third of their population within a single breeding season. Two sea lions from a South American sea lion breeding colony. Martín Brogger Current evidence suggests H5N1 also caused mass deaths in southern elephant seals – the same species as Neil the seal – with more than 17,000 pups dying at Península Valdés in Argentina. Scientists still don’t know how many adults died. Our team of researchers – from the Universidad Nacional del Comahue in Argentina and Deakin University in Australia – documented a dramatic decline in the number of seals in northern Patagonia following the 2022-23 outbreak. Subsequent studies across South America show infected pinnipeds developed severe neurological and respiratory disease. Symptoms include lethargy, tremors, impaired coordination and laboured breathing, among others. Affected animals showed severe respiratory disease and neurological signs, and post-mortem examinations revealed marked lung lesions. Many animals died within a short period after clinical signs appeared. Read more: The warning signs are over: Australia now faces a devastating bird flu outbreak in wildlife Australian mammals at risk Though confronting, the South American outbreak gives us crucial insight into how H5N1 spreads, which species may be most vulnerable and what strategies could reduce its impacts. Each time H5N1 infects and replicates in a mammal, the virus becomes better at adapting to mammalian hosts. Monitoring how efficiently it spreads between mammals is therefore essential for protecting wildlife. It also allows us to assess the risk of human infection — which currently remains low — and the potential for a broader pandemic. Two Australian sea lions (Neophoca cinerea) resting on a beach. Henrik Karlsson/Getty For now, H5N1 has not yet reached Australia’s pinniped colonies, which are already under pressure from fishery nets and hooks, pollution, habitat destruction and climate change. So we still have time to protect them from H5N1. Authorities should start with Kangaroo Island, where infected seabirds have been found near the breeding habitat of the endangered Australian sea lion. Other threatened marine mammals may also be vulnerable. This includes the rare Burrunan dolphin, of which there are less than 200 individual animals swimming around Victoria’s Port Phillip Bay and Gippsland regions. There are fewer than 200 Burrunan dolphins left in the wild. tracielouise/Getty So, how can we protect them? As Australia’s number of confirmed H5N1 cases rises, urgent action is needed to protect our vulnerable marine mammals. Australian authorities can learn from the South American outbreak by: frequently conducting population censuses, to detect unusual deaths and sudden changes in the size of seal and sea lion colonies closely monitoring live animals and taking samples of any dead animals, to track how the virus is circulating before any mass deaths happen removing all carcasses, particularly near tourist areas, to stop scavenging birds, dogs and animals from being exposed to infected animals ensuring researchers, wildlife managers and tourism operators stick to strict biosecurity protocols, such as wearing appropriate personal protective equipment when handling sick or dead wildlife and disinfecting boots and equipment between sites tightening biosecurity measures around food production, particularly intensive poultry farms where commercial poultry may be exposed to infected wild birds. The public can also help protect our vulnerable pinnipeds by: not approaching any sick wildlife keeping pets away from wildlife reporting any sightings of sick or dead birds, seals, sea lions or other animals to the 24-hour Emergency Animal Disease Hotline by ringing 1800 675 888, noting details about the date, location, type and number of animals. As the number of infected seabirds rises, so does the threat of a H5N1 outbreak among Australia’s marine mammal colonies. South America reveals how devastating this virus can be for entire ecosystems. Australia should heed that warning while there is still time to protect our precious pinnipeds. Read more: Scavenger animals are the missing link in Australia’s bird flu response. Three experts explain Correction: This article originally stated post-mortem examinations of infected pinnipeds revealed the virus directly affected animals’ brains and lungs, and could lead to death within a short period. This has been corrected to say post-mortem examinations of infected pinnipeds revealed marked lung lesions, and many of them died within a short period after clinical signs appeared. Full necropsies were not carried out on the Argentinian seals due to biosecurity concerns, meaning the cause of death cannot be definitively attributed to the virus. analysis.event: H5N1 bird flu has been detected in wild birds across mainland Australia, with the first instance of mass death among greater crested terns off South Australia’s south-east coast. analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: At least 30,000 South American sea lions died in Peru, Chile, Argentina, Uruguay and Brazil during the outbreak. analysis.brief_en: A news report from The Conversation, published on August 4, 2026, discusses the spread of H5N1 bird flu in South America and its potential impact on Australia’s marine mammals. The article highlights that H5N1 has caused mass deaths among pinnipeds, including southern elephant seals in Argentina, with over 17,000 pups dying. In South America, the virus has led to the death of at least 30,000 sea lions in several countries. The report warns that H5N1 could spread to Australia’s pinnipeds, which are already under threat from other environmental factors. Authorities in Australia are monitoring the situation, with the first confirmed mass death of greater crested terns reported off the south-east coast of South Australia. The article emphasizes the need for biosecurity measures to prevent the virus from reaching Australia’s marine mammal colonies, which are vulnerable due to their ecological and conservation status. news.content_zh: The Conversation 于 2026 年 8 月 4 日发表的一篇新闻报道讨论了 H5N1 禽流感在南美洲的传播及其对澳大利亚海洋哺乳动物的潜在影响。文章强调,H5N1 病毒已导致鳍足类动物大规模死亡,其中包括阿根廷的南象海豹,有超过 17,000 只幼崽死亡。在南美洲,该病毒已导致多个国家至少 30,000 只海狮死亡。该报告警告说,H5N1 病毒可能会传播到澳大利亚的鳍足类动物,而这些动物已经受到其他环境因素的威胁。澳大利亚当局正在密切关注事态发展,南澳大利亚东南海岸首次确认大凤头燕鸥大规模死亡。文章强调需要采取生物安全措施,以防止病毒到达澳大利亚海洋哺乳动物群落,这些哺乳动物群落因其生态和保护状况而脆弱。它还指出,虽然人类感染的风险仍然很低,但该病毒适应哺乳动物 宿主 的能力是潜在更广泛的 暴发 的担忧。

surprised when the virus, which is common in wild birds, was discovered in dairy cattle, poultry, and even people. (WWMT) 2Comment Share topics: Michigan Birdflu Biosecurity GAAMPs MDARD Emergencyorders Farmers Publiccomment LANSING, Mich. — The emergency biosecurity mandates that swept Michigan farms during the 2024 avian influenza outbreak could soon become permanently integrated into state agricultural guidelines. The Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development (MDARD) is currently reviewing its annual edits to the Generally Accepted Agricultural and Management Practices, commonly known as GAAMPs, and Generally Accepted Processing Practices (GAPPs). This year's draft includes a variety of best-practice updates, including recommending farmers implement and document biosecurity measures, to prevent the spread of diseases. According to an officials from MDARD and MSU Extension, it is ideal for commercial farms of any size to have both a daily safety protocol and to establish reliable emergency response strategies, in case of abnormal outbreaks. Draft 2027 GAAMPs summary of proposed changesPDF previewPreview PDF View PDF Previous Coverage: Michigan farms help USDA in research of bird flu outbreak spreading to cattle and humans State-issued emergency orders in 2024 required commercial dairy and poultry operations to immediately increase biosecurity to combat bird flu. Many farmers were left scrambling to implement new protocol. Agricultural officials say emergency actions are necessary to contain the spread of disease, but daily biosecurity measures play an important role in prevention. Among the recommendations drafted in this year's GAAMPs, they are suggesting farmers formalize, on paper, their own approach to daily and emergency biosecurity. Between COVID-19 and bird flu to recent cyclophorias cases, many have come to realize the importance of preventing and responding to widespread disease outbreaks. That's something MDARD says the state is focused on, too. While MDARD does have authority to address emergency situations, however, the GAAMPs or GAPPs are intended to serve a more general purpose, and are not specific to any outbreak or disease. Moreover, they are simply suggestions. MDARD'S GAAMPs and GAPPs coordinator, Kyle McCarty, points out that these updates are aimed at promoting best practices and prevent public nuisance, as part of an effort to promote a positive image of agriculture in Michigan. An MSU Extension spokesperson said these measures prepare the state, not just for known viruses, but for diseases the industry has yet to encounter. Because modern food sources are highly interconnected, tracking and containment are crucial to pinpointing the origin of an outbreak before it spreads. The updated guidelines encourage farmers to maintain baseline daily biosecurity protocols, including fences and barriers, alongside a heightened security plan that can be enacted immediately if an outbreak occurs, such as changing boots and clothing before and after leaving secure areas of their farms and restricting visitors. "They're voluntary practices that operations of any size could be implementing," McCarty said. More news in West Michigan: What a psychologist wants you to know about the Grand Haven family murder-suicide Because writing a biosecurity plan from scratch can be overwhelming, the GAAMPs committee drafted 'Appendix A' to serve as a template that farm operators can use to start building their own plan, officials said. It is divided into key action areas: Designation of a Biosecurity Manager: The plan requires the farm to explicitly name the individual (often the owner or herd manager) who is responsible for developing, implementing, and enforcing the biosecurity protocols. Line of Separation (LOS): This requires defining a clear physical or imaginary line that separates the "clean" areas of the farm (where the animals are) from the "dirty" areas (outside world). It asks how the farm plans to enforce this (e.g., gates, signage, locked doors) and how workers transition across this line. Personnel and Visitor Protocols: Sign-in logs for keeping track of who enters the facility; disposable boot covers, footbaths, or dedicated clothing for farm; Downtime requirements for workers who have been exposed to other farm animals. Animal Movement and Isolation: Protocols for quarantining new animals for a set period (usually 14-30 days) before introducing them to the group. Dead Stock Management: Procedures for disposing of deceased animals in a way that prevents scavengers and disease spread. Equipment and Vehicles: Guidelines for cleaning and disinfecting shared equipment before use, especially if they are borrowed from a neighboring farm. Wildlife, Rodent, and Pest Control: Securing feed bins from wild birds, cleaning spills, and managing standing water. Beyond biosecurity on farms, the proposed GAAMPs draft proposes several other updates, such as new spacing between honeybee colonies and recommendations for greenhouses, to prevent potential complaints around noise or light pollution. State officials are actively seeking feedback on the new recommendations to determine how they will affect farmers. Residents and farmers are encouraged to review the draft and provide input before the public comment period closes at the end of August. The announcement from MDARD said public input can be submitted in multiple ways, including: Email: MDARD-RTF@michigan.gov Website: Submit comments on the GAAMPs and/or on the GAPPs U.S. Mail: Send written comments to the MDARD Right to Farm Program, P.O. Box 30017, Lansing, MI 48909 Public Meeting: A virtual public meeting is scheduled for August 27, 2026, at 1 p.m. ET | Link to join the virtual meeting READ THE COMMENTS (2) MDARD will forward all public input received by August 30 deadline, and the respective advisory committees will share their recommendations at the regularly scheduled Michigan Commission of Agriculture and Rural Development meeting on September 9, 2026. Home Arts + Culture Economy Education Environment + Energy Ethics + Religion Health Politics + Society Science + Tech World Podcasts Local En Español Edition Africa Australia Brasil Canada Canada (français) Català España Europe France Global Indonesia New Zealand United Kingdom United States Donate Skip to content Edition: United States Africa Australia Brasil Canada Canada (français) Català España Europe France Global Indonesia New Zealand United Kingdom s Donate Newsletters Academic rigor, journalistic flair Arts + Culture Economy Education Environment + Energy Ethics + Religion Health Politics + Society Science + Tech World Podcasts Local Auscape/Getty Why Australia should urgently vaccinate wildlife most at risk from H5N1 bird flu Published: August 5, 2026 4:09pm EDT Australia has confirmed deadly H5N1 bird flu has been found in 102 wild seabirds across five states at the time of writing, including the country’s first mass death of birds. The question is no longer if this virus can harm Australian wildlife, but whether we should use every available tool to protect species most at risk. Vaccination cannot stop H5N1 spreading through wildlife. But it could prevent an outbreak from killing all of the at-risk species in an area – a tragic local extinction. Australia should begin targeted vaccination of threatened birds. It should also urgently develop a strategy for seals and sea lions, rather than waiting until thousands are dead. A policy exists, but action remains too cautious Australia has a national policy that allows emergency vaccination of rare, protected and valuable birds, including animals in zoos, sanctuaries, breeding programs and some managed wild populations. The government has also purchased an inactivated H5 vaccine – containing no live virus – and is running pilot studies in captive non-poultry birds. This is important groundwork, but not yet a public program comparable with New Zealand’s ambitious and proactive approach to vaccinate five of the country’s rarest birds before the arrival of H5N1. Australian zoos and sanctuaries have received funding to strengthen biosecurity and captive “insurance populations”. Pilot vaccinations are underway, but the government has not announced which threatened species will receive wider vaccination, where, or when. More importantly, the policy excludes non-avian (bird) species, meaning marine mammals are not considered despite their known vulnerability to H5N1. No plans have been announced to the public for Australian vaccination trials for seals or sea lions. What overseas programs show New Zealand prepared before H5N1 arrived. After species-specific trials, it began vaccinating about 300 core breeding birds of rare species, including kākāpō, takahē and black stilts. These are captive or closely managed populations whose individuals can be found, vaccinated twice and monitored. The United States acted after H5N1 killed 21 critically endangered California condors. By October 2024, 207 captive and free-flying condors had been vaccinated. The vaccine was judged safe, although two birds had treatable adverse reactions. France has conducted a vaccine trial in wild king penguin chicks on the French sub-Antarctic island of Crozet. The vaccine produced strong, virus-neutralising antibodies without detected adverse effects. These programs do not prove vaccination will prevent every infection. But it could lessen severe disease and reduce the number of animals that die in threatened populations. The marine mammals most at risk are the sea lion, fur seal and elephant seal, while the Tasmanian devil and eastern quoll (pictured) are the highest-risk species on land. Rexness/flickr, CC BY Which species should Australia vaccinate? Broadscale vaccination of free-ranging wildlife is unrealistic. Most H5 vaccines require two doses, and most wildlife is difficult to capture once, let alone being recaptured for a booster and blood test. The best candidates are small populations of at-risk species that are either easily accessible or already under management. For example, threatened birds in zoos or breeding centres, or small, known colonies with tracking or regular handling. On Tuesday, the Australian government released a list of at-risk species, that showed almost one-in-five Australian bird and mammal species is at high, very high or extreme risk from the virus. Five bird species are at extreme risk – the Christmas Island frigate bird, Houtman albatross, Herald petrel, imperial shag on Heard Island and imperial shag on Macquarie Island. The marine mammals most at risk are the sea lion, fur seal and elephant seal, while the Tasmanian devil and eastern quoll are the highest risk species on land. Decisions must balance extinction risk, exposure to the virus, cost, vaccine performance, whether enough animals can be reached, and whether capture would cause unacceptable stress. Vaccination must sit alongside existing biosecurity, surveillance and conservation measures – not replace them. Australia needs a seal plan H5N1 has decimated seal and sea lion populations across South America and the Southern Ocean. More than 17,000 southern elephant seal pups were killed in Argentina in 2023. An estimated 13,359 pups died at the Australian sub-Antarctic Heard Island in 2025, believed to be from the virus. Southern elephant seals were listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List in April, in part because of the catastrophic mortality caused by bird flu. It will take decades for these populations to recover. Australia’s most vulnerable seals include the endangered Australian sea lion, Australian and long-nosed fur seals, and southern elephant seals. H5N1-positive terns have already been found at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island, home to a major Australian sea lion breeding colony. Southern elephant seals have a large breeding colony on Australia’s sub-Antarctic Macquarie Island, which remains free of H5N1 at this time. There is currently no bird flu vaccine designed specifically for marine mammals. A United States trial aimed at protecting endangered Hawaiian monk seals found a vaccine developed for cattle was safe in northern elephant seals and produced measurable antibodies. This was the closest comparable species for which a safe, conditionally licensed vaccine was available. Developing and approving a separate vaccine for every wildlife species is costly and time-consuming, so conservation programs commonly adapt vaccines already approved for domestic animals. Now is the time to act Australia should identify priority seal colonies now, trial candidate vaccines in a suitable surrogate species and plan how vaccination could be deployed. We should not wait to learn how susceptible these animals are by watching more mass deaths unfold. Vaccination is not a silver bullet. But when a disease can erase years of conservation work in weeks, we should not wait for perfect certainty. It’s time to act before catastrophe. Amazon case rekindles scientific debate Tiago Mota e Silva 17 Jul 2026 Quickly stay updated with our news shorts Tree cover is not the same as ecological recovery Rhett Ayers Butler 7 Aug 2026 Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries. A harpy eagle needs large trees for nesting and enough surrounding forest for its young to learn to fly. The Amazon also depends on the eagle. By controlling populations of monkeys, sloths, and other animals, the predator helps limit damage to the forest canopy. Its decline can therefore indicate broader changes in the ecosystem. Governments often assess biodiversity by counting species. These figures are useful, although they don’t show whether an ecosystem is still functioning. A recent paper in Frontiers in Science argues that conservation policy should also track ecological processes, including predation, migration, pollination, and the movement of water and nutrients, reports Mongabay’s John Cannon. The authors propose using the Three Global Conditions Framework, developed in 2019, to decide what different landscapes require. It divides the planet according to the degree of human influence. Large, relatively intact areas need protection from new development. Landscapes where farming and settlements coexist with nature require management that maintains ecological functions. Heavily altered areas need restoration. The approach could help countries meet the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which calls for the loss of nature to be halted and reversed by 2030. Progress varies widely among countries. The agreement is not legally binding, and national governments determine how its targets are applied. The paper uses the term “nature positive” to describe an outcome in which ecosystems are healthier at the end of the decade than they were at its start. Measuring this will be difficult. An increase in tree cover, for example, may reveal little about whether a restored forest supports its former species or ecological relationships. Implementation also raises political and economic questions. Conservation measures can restrict access to land, change farming practices, or impose costs on communities that contributed little to biodiversity loss. Decisions about what to protect and restore will depend partly on whose knowledge is recognized and who bears the expense. The framework helps distinguish among landscapes and identify suitable forms of intervention. Governments will still need to turn broad targets into policies that reflect local conditions, maintain ecological functions, and allocate costs in ways that affected communities consider fair.
