On a Philippine beach, villagers are stepping up to save sea turtle nests Mongabay.com 6 Aug 2026 Beaches in San Vicente municipality in the Philippines’ Palawan province are crucial nesting grounds for olive ridley sea turtles. But the turtles and their babies face perilous journeys on those beaches — from dogs, tourism, and increasingly severe storms and high tides. To counter these threats, the NGO Large Marine Vertebrates Research Institute Philippines (LAMAVE) has partnered with residents to patrol the beaches and rescue turtle eggs, reports contributor Rachel Duckett for Mongabay. In Santo Niño village, volunteers and patrollers conduct intensive night patrols covering more than 8 kilometers (5 mile) of the beach in five shifts. When the patrollers find a nesting turtle, they protect her from dogs. When she’s done nesting, they measure her and take photographs of her before she reenters the water. These help them identify her in the future. Then they relocate the eggs to protected hatcheries, a move researchers say is vital because nests left on the beach are almost always lost to stray dogs or flooding. Sometimes, they encounter dead nesting mothers or turtles mortally wounded by dogs. They remove eggs from those nests as well. “In the end, even though she’s dead, at least her babies survive,” said researcher Klara Simon at LAMAVE. In the hatcheries, the eggs are placed in nests in the sand, which the researchers check on every few hours. Baby olive ridleys (Lepidochelys olivacea) start emerging two months after the eggs are laid. According to LAMAVE data from last season and preliminary data from this season, their hatcheries achieve a hatching success rate of approximately 75%. For comparison, on beaches untouched by predators, hatching success rates of 80% or higher are common for olive ridley nests. Local patrollers like Jerald Mahusay, who once viewed turtle eggs as toys during his childhood, now serve as research assistants and patrol leaders. LAMAVE also engages directly with residents to manage free-roaming dogs, such as building enclosures for pets that might otherwise attack turtles and eat the eggs. Despite the current reliance on hatcheries, project leader Kalei Suza said relocation is a temporary measure necessitated by human-induced pressures. “We still want the turtles to nest in their regular, natural place where they want to nest, because mama knows best,” Suza said, noting that the ultimate goal is for the community to take full ownership of turtle protection. San Vicente has seen a rise in tourism over the last few years. Luxury developer Century Properties purchased 56 hectares (138 acres) of land in the municipality with plans to build a beachfront resort. Another major developer, Megaworld Corporation, has begun construction of a resort expected to cover 462 hectares (1,142 acres). Read the full story by Rachel Duckett here. Banner image: LAMAVE patrollers find a predated nest in Santo Niño, San Vicente, Palawan, April 2026. Image by Rachel Duckett for Mongabay. In Manila’s shadow, a forest refuge still shelters rare plants Naina Rao 6 Aug 2026 A mountainous reserve near Manila, the Philippine capital, is a critical ecological refuge, harboring high levels of plant diversity despite its proximity to the highly urbanized city, according to a recent study. The findings come from surveys done 10 years earlier, however, and mounting pressures on the area’s forests since then may have had an impact, the authors say. As the last remaining natural lowland forest in Cavite province, on the southern shores of Manila Bay, Mounts Palay-palay-Mataas-na-Gulod Protected Landscape serves as a vital stronghold for Philippine biodiversity, researchers say. In July 2016, they surveyed plants within the landscape, known as MPPMGPL. At the time, they documented 294 species of plants across the landscape’s varied habitats, from grasslands and secondary forests to old-growth stands. They found that 42 species, or 16%, are found only in the Philippines, while 31 species are classified as threatened on national or international red lists. “The most remarkable finding is that this landscape ... harbors an incredibly high concentration of biodiversity despite being so close to highly urbanized zones,” study lead author Enrico Replan, an assistant professor at the Institute of Environmental Science and Meteorology (IESM) at the University of the Philippines Diliman, told Mongabay by email. The study also identified 43 species that likely represent new records for Cavite province, “filling major geographic knowledge gaps,” Replan said. Among the most significant findings was the dominance of guijo (Shorea guiso), a critically endangered tree species, in the forest’s interior core. This highlights the role of MPPMGPL as a key conservation refuge, the authors write. While the study was only published recently, Replan told Mongabay the 2016 findings offer a baseline for this landscape; there haven’t been similar surveys since. In the past 10 years, however, urbanization and land conversion have led to a decrease in forested areas and breached strict protection zones in the landscape. A study that used satellite imagery to examine changes in forest area from 2015 to 2021, found a 13.8% decrease in MPPMGPL due to urbanization. The 2016 survey “showed promising resurgence of Shorea guiso” in the interior core parts of MPPMGPL, Replan said. But because dipterocarp species such as guijo are highly sensitive to local climatic changes and canopy gaps, he added that any encroachment that disturbed the forest over the last decade could easily have stalled this progress. “This 10-year gap highlights exactly why we are calling for continuous, long-term monitoring rather than relying solely on spatial snapshots,” Replan said. He added that stricter local policy interventions and aggressive conservation programs are urgently needed to safeguard the endemic and threatened plants in the landscape “before they are permanently fragmented or lost.” The research team writes that establishing permanent monitoring plots would better track the functional dynamics of this ecosystem amidst climate change. Banner image: Enrico Replan from the, Assistant Professor at the Institute of Environmental Science and Meteorology (IESM), University of the Philippines Diliman doing fieldwork in Mounts Palay-Palay-Mataas-na-Gulod Protected Landscape. Image courtesy of Enrico Replan. What happens after a whale strands on a Mumbai beach? Stephin Thomas 6 Aug 2026 On the morning of June 27, a 7.6-meter (25-foot) blue whale calf washed ashore on a busy beach in Mumbai, India’s financial capital and the capital of Maharashtra state. Whale strandings are rare along the Maharashtra coast, so Mongabay spoke with experts to find out what happened next. “Each stranding incident is a totally unexpected event,” N. Vasudevan, former head of Maharashtra government’s Mangrove Cell, an administrative unit that manages coastal ecosystems, told Mongabay. “You can prepare for years, but then it may not happen for years. And one fine morning, it is there on the beach.” According to the Mangrove Foundation, a registered society established by the Maharashtra government, only six of the 109 recorded stranding incidents in 2020-21 involved whales. Under national guidelines, the first step in any stranding involving a protected species, such as the blue whale (Balaenoptera musculus), is alerting the local stranding network, whose coordinator notifies the forest department, according to Shaunak Modi, director of the Coastal Conservation Foundation, which is also part of the Mumbai Stranding Response Network. Modi said that on June 27, a lifeguard notified him about the whale calf around 9 a.m. By the time he reached the site in the Bandra coastline 30 minutes later, the young cetacean had suffered severe injuries from crashing against exposed rocks. Ultimately, police and fire department authorities at the site confirmed it had died. Fishers and local people told Modi they had first spotted the stranded whale around 6 a.m. First responders, primarily local fishers and lifeguards, receive specialized training to inform the network immediately of these emergencies, he said. But what happens to the dead whale? Modi said legal and practical realities clash under national law. The blue whale is a Schedule 1 species, meaning authorities give it the highest-level protection in India. “As per the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, if any Schedule 1 species dies, it needs to be cremated,” Modi said. But the law was made with terrestrial animals in mind, he added. “If you try to burn a whale, I can assure you it will keep burning for days, if not weeks, because it has that much oil in it. So then instead of cremating a marine mammal, they’re buried.” The calf was buried in a Mumbai beach. Beforehand, veterinarians collected tissue samples and conducted a necropsy under forest department supervision. “The necropsy report is still not ready, but what we know is that it was a calf,” Modi said. “Blue whale calves stay with their mother for up to seven or eight years and are entirely dependent on her for food during the first few years. We assume it may have been separated from its mother, which caused its condition.” Vasudevan said there are systematic hurdles in knowing the cause of death. “The experts who conduct necropsy are nonexistent in our country.” Banner image: Stranded whale calf in Mumbai. Image courtesy of Shaunak Modi. Social media images lead to first recording of parasitoid wasp species in Japan David Brown 6 Aug 2026 Photos of a striking, iridescent wasp posted on social media by wasp enthusiasts in Japan have led to an unexpected discovery: The images are the first record of the species in Japan. The footage also helped scientists describe a male of the species for the first time. The images and a video of the wasps were posted by two citizen scientists on Twitter (now X) in 2018 and 2021. The video showed a female wasp depositing her eggs onto a hard egg case of a praying mantis. Taisuke Kawano, a wasp expert at the Kyushu University Museum, Japan, noticed the footage and contacted the wasp enthusiasts who then sent him a few specimens of the wasp. The citizen scientists are also co-authors of a study, published in June, that details the scientists’ findings. Kawano and his colleagues identified the wasp as Eupelmus curvator. It’s a parasitoid wasp that lays its eggs in the egg cases of mantises. The larvae of the wasps feed on the mantis eggs as they develop. The researchers said the photos posted on social media are the first known record of Eupelmus curvator in Japan. The species was previously known only from China. The researchers were also able to scientifically describe the E. curvator male for the first time. Only the female of the species was previously described. The 2016 survey “showed promising resurgence of Shorea guiso” in the interior core parts of MPPMGPL, Replan said. But because dipterocarp species such as guijo are highly sensitive to local climatic changes and canopy gaps, he added that any encroachment that disturbed the forest over the last decade could easily have stalled this progress. “This 10-year gap highlights exactly why we are calling for continuous, long-term monitoring rather than relying solely on spatial snapshots,” Replan said. He added that stricter local policy interventions and aggressive conservation programs are urgently needed to safeguard the endemic and threatened plants in the landscape “before they are permanently fragmented or lost.” The research team writes that establishing permanent monitoring plots would better track the functional dynamics of this ecosystem amidst climate change. Banner image: Enrico Replan from the, Assistant Professor at the Institute of Environmental Science and Meteorology (IESM), University of the Philippines Diliman doing fieldwork in Mounts Palay-Palay-Mataas-na-Gulod Protected Landscape. Image courtesy of Enrico Replan. What happens after a whale strands on a Mumbai beach? Stephin Thomas 6 Aug 2026 On the morning of June 27, a 7.6-meter (25-foot) blue whale calf washed ashore on a busy beach in Mumbai, India’s financial capital and the capital of Maharashtra state. Whale strandings are rare along the Maharashtra coast, so Mongabay spoke with experts to find out what happened next. “Each stranding incident is a totally unexpected event,” N. Vasudevan, former head of Maharashtra government’s Mangrove Cell, an administrative unit that manages coastal ecosystems, told Mongabay. “You can prepare for years, but then it may not happen for years. And one fine morning, it is there on the beach.” According to the Mangrove Foundation, a registered society established by the Maharashtra government, only six of the 109 recorded stranding incidents in 2020-21 involved whales. Under national guidelines, the first step in any stranding involving a protected species, such as the blue whale (Balaenoptera musculus), is alerting the local stranding network, whose coordinator notifies the forest department, according to Shaunak Modi, director of the Coastal Conservation Foundation, which is also part of the Mumbai Stranding Response Network. Modi said that on June 27, a lifeguard notified him about the whale calf around 9 a.m. By the time he reached the site in the Bandra coastline 30 minutes later, the young cetacean had suffered severe injuries from crashing against exposed rocks. Ultimately, police and fire department authorities at the site confirmed it had died. Fishers and local people told Modi they had first spotted the stranded whale around 6 a.m. First responders, primarily local fishers and lifeguards, receive specialized training to inform the network immediately of these emergencies, he said. But what happens to the dead whale? Modi said legal and practical realities clash under national law. The blue whale is a Schedule 1 species, meaning authorities give it the highest-level protection in India. “As per the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, if any Schedule 1 species dies, it needs to be cremated,” Modi said. But the law was made with terrestrial animals in mind, he added. “If you try to burn a whale, I can assure you it will keep burning for days, if not weeks, because it has that much oil in it. So then instead of cremating a marine mammal, they’re buried.” The calf was buried in a Mumbai beach. Beforehand, veterinarians collected tissue samples and conducted a necropsy under forest department supervision. “The necropsy report is still not ready, but what we know is that it was a calf,” Modi said. “Blue whale calves stay with their mother for up to seven or eight years and are entirely dependent on her for food during the first few years. We assume it may have been separated from its mother, which caused its condition.” Vasudevan said there are systematic hurdles in knowing the cause of death. “The experts who conduct necropsy are nonexistent in our country.” Banner image: Stranded whale calf in Mumbai. Image courtesy of Shaunak Modi. Social media images lead to first recording of parasitoid wasp species in Japan David Brown 6 Aug 2026 Photos of a striking, iridescent wasp posted on social media by wasp enthusiasts in Japan have led to an unexpected discovery: The images are the first record of the species in Japan. The footage also helped scientists describe a male of the species for the first time. The images and a video of the wasps were posted by two citizen scientists on Twitter (now X) in 2018 and 2021. The video showed a female wasp depositing her eggs onto a hard egg case of a praying mantis. Taisuke Kawano, a wasp expert at the Kyushu University Museum, Japan, noticed the footage and contacted the wasp enthusiasts who then sent him a few specimens of the wasp. The citizen scientists are also co-authors of a study, published in June, that details the scientists’ findings. Kawano and his colleagues identified the wasp as Eupelmus curvator. It’s a parasitoid wasp that lays its eggs in the egg cases of mantises. The larvae of the wasps feed on the mantis eggs as they develop. The researchers said the photos posted on social media are the first known record of Eupelmus curvator in Japan. The species was previously known only from China. The researchers were also able to scientifically describe the E. curvator male for the first time. Only the female of the species was previously described. Slide 1 of 3 Jetstar fees The airline will charge passengers to stow carry-on luggage in overhead lockers from next year. Only a small under-seat bag will be allowed at no extra cost. The cost will start at $25 per domestic one-way flight, while the add-on could be an extra $52 for an international flight. Slide 1 of 4 Alan Jones trial Alan Jones has gone on trial accused of indecent assault and sexual touching. Six young men allege he engaged in inappropriate conduct. Mr Jones denies the charges. His defence says the case is about media rivalry and treachery. Slide 1 of 3 FIFA latest European football body UEFA has threatened legal action over FIFA president Gianni Infantino's failed plan to sell a stake in future World Cup profits. The plan would have raised $US4.2 billion ($5.9 billion) by selling about 20 per cent of a new unit that would run events, including the World Cup. UEFA led the backlash against Mr Infantino, with its 55 member federations agreeing to boycott all FIFA events and competitions while the proposal was active. Slide 1 of 3 Bird flu A mass mortality incident has been confirmed among Australian birds. It's the first linked to the H5 bird flu outbreak. The incident was confirmed among terns off South Australia's coast. Slide 1 of 3 EVs surge Australia has recorded its biggest-ever surge in electric vehicle sales. Across April, May and June, nearly one in every two vehicles sold was either electric or hybrid. But from April next year, the tax exemption on EVs will begin to roll back. For the second year in a row, visitors to the Butler Farm Show can expect to see the finest live duck, chicken and turkey exhibits — but only from a safe distance. Jordan Kennedy, who is in charge of poultry events at the Butler Farm Show, said event organizers are following Pennsylvania guidelines on managing highly pathologic avian influenza, or HPAI. The guidelines were slightly loosened last year, just enough to allow the farm show to include poultry showmanship for the first time since 2019. “The farm show is doing everything it can to give opportunities to families and kids; and we’re doing everything we can within the Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture's requirements to allow these kids to show and exhibit the animals they work so hard on,” Kennedy said. Ken Metrick, Butler Farm Show board secretary, was in charge of the Butler County 4-H Poultry Club in 2019. He has chickens at his Harvest View Farm in Butler Township. Butler Eagle File Photo As a result of restrictions imposed by the Department of Agriculture, the public will not be allowed into the poultry tent, but will be allowed to look at the birds from a distance. “The Department of Agriculture requires us to have a buffer or quarantine zone between the birds and the public, so there will be no public allowed to go into the poultry tent,” Kennedy said. “We're going to try and have the tent as open as possible so that folks can see into the tent.” Visitors can rest assured all birds exhibited at the Farm Show are prescreened for avian flu and other illnesses, according to Kennedy. “Every bird that's on the grounds that's being exhibited has to be tested for diseases and sicknesses, including avian influenza, just to ensure that all the birds and people are as safe as possible,” Kennedy said. Due to tighter restrictions against avian influenza, poultry exhibits were entirely absent from the farm show from 2021 to 2024. Combined with the 2020 show, which was canceled entirely due to the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, that marked five straight seasons in which Butler County’s young poultry farmers were unable to display their work at the farm show. During those years, the farm show filled the poultry tent with educational displays and posters. While they may have a tough time getting a good look at what’s going on, visitors can look forward to the traditional poultry showcases this year, as well as a new one: market turkey. The poultry show is scheduled at 9 a.m. Tuesday, Aug. 11, with poultry showmanship scheduled for 9 a.m. the following day. “We have our usual poultry show where the show birds will be judged,” Kennedy said. “All your different breeds and ages of poultry, whether it be large chicken, bantam chicken, large duck, bantam duck, geese, turkeys.” Lily Williams, a Butler Area High School junior, shows off the Butler County 4-H poultry club’s turkey on Saturday, Aug. 9, 2025, at the Butler Farm Show. The bird was 35 pounds and 17 weeks old. Matthew Glover/Butler Eagle In addition, turkeys and meat pens (a type of chicken) are among the types of livestock which will be auctioned off at the Farm Show’s annual Junior Livestock Sale on Thursday, Aug. 13. Unlike the poultry tent, the livestock sale will be open to the public. “Those turkeys will be shown by the kids, judged by an official judge and then sold Thursday night at the livestock auction,” Kennedy said. This year’s Farm Show also marks the return of two popular poultry-related events — the rooster crowing contest, scheduled for 4 p.m. Wednesday, Aug. 12, and the poultry costume contest, scheduled for 4 p.m. Friday, Aug. 14. While the costume contest has been around for “quite a few years” according to Kennedy, the rooster crowing contest is entering its second year after a successful debut in 2025. “The 4-H Poultry Club has grown and is still growing,” Kennedy said. “The rooster crowing contest and the costume contest are both set up to give these kids another opportunity to work with their animals and enjoy themselves. We hope that as many kids as possible participate, but it's a busy week for a lot of those kids.” Keira Cardin plays sounds from her phone to get her rooster to crow during the rooster crowing contest at the 77th annual Butler Farm Show on Wednesday, Aug. 6, 2025. supplementary_news.content: 比公众号更快、更全的新闻APP 登录 / 注册 退出 头条 时事 侨闻 深度 直播 文化 财经 生活 专题 视频 求职 头条限定 [退出登录] 取消 头条 时事 侨闻 深度 直播 文化 财经 生活 专题 视频 求职 头条限定 在线电子报 联系我们 安卓下载 IOS下载 澳大利亚首次确认H5N1致海鸟大规模死亡,当局警惕疫情扩散 2026/08/03 来源:网络编辑 微信扫一扫:分享 微信里点“发现”,扫一下 二维码便可将本文分享至朋友圈。 (亚太快讯消息)澳大利亚政府3日宣布,国内首次确认发生H5N1型高致病性禽流感导致海鸟大规模死亡事件,并警告疫情存在进一步扩散的风险。此次事件发生在南澳大利亚州阿德莱德以南近海,当地发现约50只大凤头燕鸥死亡。 不过,目前禽流感尚未在养鸡场等农场发现感染病例。自今年6月澳大利亚首次确认H5N1疫情以来,为保护家禽安全,许多农场已采取封闭管理等防疫措施。 澳大利亚农业部长柯林斯表示,7月31日,工作人员在距离阿德莱德约250公里的凯普贾法附近海域岩礁上发现49只死亡和35只患病的大凤头燕鸥,经检测均确认感染H5N1病毒。 据日本媒体综合报道,柯林斯在接受媒体采访时表示,这是澳大利亚首次确认因H5N1禽流感导致海鸟大规模死亡,“情况显然令人高度担忧”。他同时警告,澳大利亚民众应做好心理准备,未来疫情可能继续扩散,并影响更多野生动物。 据柯林斯介绍,截至目前,澳大利亚已累计确认74例H5N1感染病例,分布范围从西澳大利亚州一直延伸至昆士兰州,其中绝大多数病例发生在南澳大利亚州。 从西澳到昆州,74例感染病例正在勾勒出一条沿澳大利亚海岸线延伸的疫情轨迹。海鸟的死亡是一个信号,提醒人们这种病毒可能正在向南半球扩散。对于长期与禽流感绝缘的澳大利亚来说,这或许是一次新的考验。 图源:路透社 澳大利亚政府3日宣布,国内首次确认发生H5N1型高致病性禽流感导致海鸟大规模死亡事件,并警告疫情存在进一步扩散的风险。此次事件发生在南澳大利亚州阿德莱德以南近海,当地发现约50只大凤头燕鸥死亡。 显示全部内容 网友评论 0 条评论 匿名评论 登录 注册 登录 注册 所有评论 显示更多评论 相关新闻 日本拟收紧外国人永住许可审查,家庭收入原则上需高于日本平均水平 “精神小伙”写《我的妈妈》获赞近300万 日本政府拟限时下调食品消费税,自民党议员质疑政策方向 台民调:赖清德不满意度高于满意度 多瑙河水位降至新低 二战军舰残骸露出水面 西班牙北非属地休达仍有逾千名无监护人未成年人,当地请求中央政府紧急支援 日本警察厅拟远程分析"匿流"头目手机 专家研讨会10日首次开会 香港特区政府终止调查壹传媒有限公司事务 绿营避绿 台地方选举前民进党参选人集体“变色”
